But other senior rabbis, many from the progressive wing of the community, have come forward to stress the diversity of views within the British Jewish community, with some backing Miliband’s sanctions, while others warned that concern about the measures should not become an excuse for ignoring settler violence and expansion, and others calling for the government to go further.

Jonathan Wittenberg, a senior rabbi of Masorti Judaism, said he was in the Palestinian village of Umm al Khair while Miliband was delivering his speech, and had seen the results of settler violence “with my own eyes”.

“What is taking place today in the West Bank is a Chillul HaShem, a violation of God’s name of the worst order. We cannot stay silent. This is terrible for Palestinian people who want to get on with their lives in peace. It is terrible for Israel,” he said.

Wittenberg added: “We must speak out. We must do so out of deep concern for what is human and just, and for the sake of Israel and Judaism. We cannot turn away.”

While he acknowledged that the British Jewish community did not have to agree with everything the British government chose to do, he said: “The time is for action.”

Rabbi Alexandra Wright from the Liberal Jewish Synagogue in London, vice-chair of the British Friends of Rabbis for Human Rights, said while not everyone in the community would support the sanctions, action was needed as “the occupation and escalating violence are harming Palestinians and Israelis”.

She said: “The sanctions are the UK’s commitment to a two-state solution. The Anglo-Jewish community is committed to a Jewish state that is founded, not on oppression and violence, but, in the words of Israel’s declaration of independence, ‘on freedom, justice and peace as envisaged by the prophets of Israel’.”

Wright, who had recently visited the Palestinian village Umm al-Khair, which has faced relentless attacks by Israeli settlers, called on the Jewish community to “not hold back any progression towards a two-state solution”.

Jeremy Gordon, the rabbi of New London Synagogue, who came out in favour of Miliband’s sanctions, said: “It is wrong to argue for silence, inaction or ‘the use of carrots’ – appeasement – before the settler movement and those who support it. The playbook of these settlers is predicated on the notion that they will be appeased or ignored, and that well-meaning Jews the world over overlook their illegal and criminal actions.”

Lev Taylor, rabbi of Kingston Liberal Synagogue in London, described the sanctions as a sign “the government is moving in the right direction”. He added: “Some of my Israeli members have been campaigning for sanctions exactly like this … The Judaism in which I believe repudiates this brutal occupation.”

He pointed to the statements from the Israeli member of the Knesset Gilad Kariv, who said: “The blame for the European countries’ announcement of sanctions falls squarely on the shoulders of [Benjamin] Netanyahu, [Bezalel] Smotrich, [Israel] Katz, and [Gideon] Sa’ar.”

There is some consternation within the Orthodox community at the suggestion British Jews are uniformly opposed to the sanctions.

Miliband, the foreign secretary, announced the sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank on Tuesday, with the government taking the position that Israel’s occupation of the Palestinian territory was unlawful.

after newsletter promotion

The measures were coordinated with France, Canada and nine other countries that were also introducing sanctions on Israel over the increasing expansion of settlements, which the UK government says is threatening the future of a Palestinian state.

Jonathan Boyd, the executive director for Institute for Jewish Policy Research, explained there are no robust survey data on whether British Jews support sanctions on Israeli settlements specifically. “However, the available evidence shows that views on Israeli government policy and the conflict are quite diverse, varying by age, denomination and political outlook.

“At the same time, they also show that most British Jews feel a strong emotional attachment to Israel and have become increasingly concerned about antisemitism in Britain since October 7.”

Rabbi Charley Baginsky and Rabbi Josh Levy, co-leaders of Progressive Judaism, which represents about one-third of Jews affiliated to synagogues and estimates the same proportion of non-affiliated Jews share its values, described sanctions as a “clumsy tool” that could have unintended consequences. But they said that “measures directed at Israeli settlements are not the same as an attack on Jews. We should take care not to collapse the distinction between them.”

They called on those against sanctions to offer more than statements condemning violence, adding: “Inaction is not neutral. It too is a political and moral choice.”

Wittenberg, Baginsky and Levy all asserted their opposition to the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement, and welcomed Miliband’s stance against it.

Tuesday’s sanctions announcement prompted a swift backlash from Israel, which ordered the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem and banned 12 British MPs and activists from entering Israel.

Washington’s ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, threatened that the US could take retaliatory action over trade, but the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US would “obviously” not follow the UK government’s actions but did not want to see the West Bank destabilised.

The UK foreign secretary said he regretted what the Israeli government had announced but was “proud of what we did yesterday and it was the right thing to do”.

Miliband accepted the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem would be “damaging” but said the government had “weighed up the costs and benefits in advance of this”.

The Guardian view on UK-EU relations: voters would reward greater ambition

The Guardian Wed, 09 Sep 2026 17:40:47 GMT

The architects of Brexit know it has failed. That presents Andy Burnham with an opportunity to set a bolder new agenda

Modesty is not a trait commonly associated with Nigel Farage. Something else must explain the Reform UK leader’s reluctance to talk about what is undoubtedly his biggest achievement.

Few individuals can boast of having influenced British politics as drastically as Mr Farage, with his record of campaigning for Brexit before that word was even coined. He will for ever be associated with the demand for emancipation from Brussels, but is rarely heard celebrating its completion. It barely earned a mention in speeches at his party’s annual conference last week. The simple reason is that none of the promises made about the benefits of life outside the EU have been fulfilled. Leaving made the country poorer, and voters know it.

Opinion polls routinely show that a majority are dissatisfied with the way Brexit has turned out. In a survey published this week by the thinktank British Future, 57% of respondents judged it to be “more a failure than a success”. Only 21% took the opposite view. There were also clear majorities in favour of closer ties when it comes to trade, defence and even health policy; 57% support a youth-mobility scheme for 18- to 30-year-olds, restoring some of the opportunities to live and work abroad that were curtailed by departure from the EU.

Those attitudes should not be confused with appetite for a complete reversal, still less a referendum to make it happen. Memories of a divisive campaign and exit process are a powerful deterrent against relitigating the question all over again.

But the balance of public opinion is skewed against the enterprise that defined Mr Farage’s political ascent and was enacted with fervour by the Conservative party. The ideological parents of Brexit are understandably embarrassed by their progeny.

That presents Andy Burnham with an opportunity. The prime minister has said he wants to be “bolder” in pursuing a closer EU relationship. He has permission from the electorate to do just that. He inherited a European “reset” from his predecessor, but it was advancing slowly. The scope of potential agreement was also limited by Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, ruling out single market and customs union membership.

Mr Burnham inherits that mandate too, and has indicated his intention to adhere to it. A UK-EU summit to advance cooperation in a range of areas – trade in agricultural goods, energy, defence and security, youth mobility – was due in July. Sir Keir’s departure led to a postponement. It has not yet been rescheduled. Technical negotiations have continued under the new government, but there is not much sense of political urgency coming from either side. That must change.

A new prime minister’s in-tray is always busy. The EU is a slow-moving apparatus. There are few incentives to grant favours to the UK when the terms of the existing Brexit deal are skewed in Brussels’ favour. Without infusions of political will from No 10, inertia will prevail.

Meanwhile, the case for closer UK-EU cooperation gets ever more compelling with each act of vandalism perpetrated by Donald Trump against the transatlantic alliance and international trading system. This strategic imperative is something the public can understand and that ideological Brexiters refuse to see. If Mr Burnham has the imagination and courage to outline an ambitious new model of UK-EU relations, he will have the majority of British voters on his side.

The Guardian view on Donald Trump’s oil deal: Venezuela pays for his vanity

The Guardian Wed, 09 Sep 2026 17:39:43 GMT

The US president seized a nation’s natural wealth in a modern-day version of gunboat diplomacy to feed his ego – not to lower Americans’ fuel bills

Imperialism does not require a flag to be planted or a governor dispatched. It can be a powerful nation deciding who governs a smaller, weaker country, and on what terms and for whose benefit its resources will be developed. Donald Trump’s kidnapping of Venezuela’s Nicolás Maduro, putting his deputy – Delcy Rodríguez – in his place as president, and then her signing a deal handing a fifth of the country’s proven oil reserves to the US, amount to a modern version of 19th-century gunboat diplomacy. Regime change supplied America’s commercial concession.

This won’t bother Mr Trump. But it should. The US president has oversold his neocolonial spoils. The additional production Venezuela is supposed to bring online might bring down oil prices eventually, but not anytime soon. Crucially, what Mr Trump calls “the biggest oil deal in history” won’t cause the price at the pump to fall before November’s midterms. When so many American voters are struggling to pay energy bills, it’s hard to see how unrealised Orinoco Belt riches are going to help Republican candidates.

The US president also promotes the idea that he is transforming the US’s industrial landscape through fossil fuels. Although the Venezuela oil grab might be highly profitable for a few selected companies, the windfall is dwarfed by the size of the US economy. Mr Trump is not getting cheap energy but a spectacle of American power. That may be enough for him.

Before Mr Maduro was captured, Mr Trump had decided that Venezuela’s oil belonged to the US. The Venezuelan strongman was offered exile if he gave Washington want it wanted. When he dithered, a US armada assembled off Venezuela’s coast. Yet Mr Trump did not replace Mr Maduro with María Corina Machado from the democratic opposition. He instead backed the authoritarian regime that could secure the oilfields from ambitious army generals and spare the costs of occupation.

The US doesn’t rule Venezuela directly, but it is exercising power through a lifelong socialist, Ms Rodríguez. She is remaking Chavismo, the revolutionary movement launched by Hugo Chávez, in her image – enraging some leftists. Ms Rodríguez has granted North American Blue Energy Partners (Nabep) concessions to 17 oilfields in Venezuela for decades to come. Nabep’s boss, Alejandro Betancourt, a controversial Venezuelan oil billionaire, popped up in Caracas for this week’s visit by the US energy secretary, Chris Wright. Nabep has in turn granted the Pentagon a 35% equity stake at no cost to the US taxpayer.

The charge of “Yankee imperialism” was often dismissed as kneejerk anti-Americanism. Mr Trump has turned it into an American boast. Ms Rodríguez argues that she is no puppet. Cooperation with Mr Trump, she says, will bring Venezuela investment and could generate $200bn in oil revenues. Unequal bargains have often benefited local rulers and intermediaries. The question is: what kind of economy and social order will that revenue produce? Oil cash is not the same as sovereign development.

Mr Trump is a playground bully handed the world’s most powerful military. He mistakes coercion for greatness and sovereign nations for toys. He uses US power to feed his bottomless ego – recently claiming himself to be a bigger historical figure than Caesar, Genghis Khan, Napoleon, Stalin and Mao. When he departs the stage, others will have to rebuild what he has squandered: the US’s authority, its alliances and its reputation.

Infantino installs loyalist to oversee Caribbean as he splits Fifa management

The Guardian Wed, 09 Sep 2026 17:17:23 GMT

Critics view Fernandes job as move to shore up position

Fifa says change is designed to make sport ‘truly global’

Gianni Infantino has separated Fifa’s management of the Caribbean countries from the rest of Concacaf in a move widely regarded by his opponents as an attempt to split the alliance to remove him from office.

Concacaf covers North and Central America as well as the Caribbean and was previously managed as one bloc. But the Guardian has learned that the former Switzerland midfielder Gelson Fernandes, an Infantino loyalist, has been appointed as the director of member associations for the Caribbean, in addition to his position looking after Fifa’s African members.

Fernandes, who played for Manchester City, Leicester and eight other clubs, joined Fifa in 2022 as director of member associations for Africa and was promoted two years later to become deputy chief members associations officer globally.

The 40-year-old works closely with Fifa’s chief members associations officer, Elkhan Mammadov, a close ally of Infantino described by many national associations as the president’s key enforcer.

Fernandes has replaced Jair Bertoni as Fifa’s liaison with the 21 Caribbean-based members, with the national associations and Concacaf informed of the change last week without consultation.

In a statement Fifa confirmed the appointment, which it said was designed to support Infantino’s vision of making the sport truly global.

“Fifa can confirm that Gelson Fernandes has taken on responsibility for the Caribbean region, in addition to his current role as regional director Africa,” it said. “With his extensive experience at Fifa and strong knowledge of football development programmes, Gelson will lead the regional team and will work closely with the member associations across the Caribbean to further support the development of football in their respective countries, following the Fifa president’s vision: making football truly global.”

Concacaf is attempting with Uefa and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) to oust Infantino. Sources at several member associations in Europe and North America regard the change as an attempt to split the Concacaf vote before March’s presidential election, with one characterising it as “an administrative war” against its president, Victor Montagliani.

The Canadian is viewed by many in Uefa as the most credible candidate to beat Infantino, although Montagliani has yet to decide whether to stand and is committed to seeking re-election as Concacaf’s president.

Infantino has stepped up his re-election campaign in the aftermath of the World Cup sell-off scandal, ignoring a written request from Montagliani to stay away from a meeting of the Caribbean Football Union (CFU) in the Dominican Republic last month.

As revealed by the Guardian, Infantino used the CFU meeting to announce approval for numerous Fifa-funded development projects for the region worth millions of dollars in what some observers described as an attempt to lobby for votes.

Mexico has split from Concacaf by announcing its support for Infantino, and losing the backing of the Caribbean would be a significant setback for those pushing to remove Infantino.

Uefa’s 55 members are believed to be united but the strength of the AFC alliance is unclear, with Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates having defied the confederation by endorsing Infantino.

Michael Gove’s reforms, rooted in a dewy-eyed vision of a mythical golden age of education that never existed, diminished arts subjects in which many students found success. The EBacc prioritised academic subjects and measurable outcomes; the arts were squeezed from timetables.

Schools knew the cost. In mainstream schools, I often saw the pride and confidence gained through performance carry over into a student’s wider learning.

I remember a father in tears of joy because he had never imagined his child with special needs performing in a school choir. I remember a mother telling me that a mainstream school production transformed her disaffected daughter’s confidence. No league table measures moments like these.

With rising numbers outside education, employment or training, we should ask whether losing such opportunities contributes to disengagement.

Music and drama are not luxuries. For many young people they provide something fundamental: a reason to believe they belong in education at all. Pete CrockettRoyal Wootton Bassett, Wiltshire

We don’t know when the centre will open because the process has been beset by delays, there is no announcement on who received the tender to manage it, and the Department for Education hasn’t officially announced that its opening is delayed yet.

I’ve spoken to the local MP about how hard this is, but nothing has changed.

There’s only one secondary school in my home town, which I was going to stay at until it dropped drama at the last minute because I was the only person in my year who’d signed up. I want a career designing costumes for theatre and film, and spend all my free time making costumes, so not doing drama wasn’t an option.

The school I now attend, Northampton School for Girls, has been hugely encouraging. It also let me travel miles away for work experience at a costume supplier for film. My old school allowed only very local placements.

Why has the country decided young people in small towns aren’t allowed to be creative? We’re pushed towards engineering or hairdressing, and told to stop wanting anything different. Molly Stubbs Brackley, Northamptonshire

It has been my privilege and honour to lead a state school that has chosen over decades to invest in the performing arts for its students. This is increasingly difficult; schools are so constrained by the curriculum and funding that it is now nigh on impossible to achieve.

Students who leave my school and continue to conservatoires or music degrees are invariably the only ones in their cohorts from the state sector. This must change to ensure our vibrant arts heritage reflects the diversity of our society in the future; besides which, young people from all backgrounds deserve to benefit from the richness participation in the arts brings us. Let’s hope Jonathan Jones’s vivid review of the Bayeux tapestry will encourage people to engage with English and British history (The Bayeux tapestry: a stupefying, thrilling, horrifying masterpiece that shakes the earth, 3 September). True (although the Germans did occupy the Channel Islands during the second world war), but he overlooks the successful invasion of 1688 when another William, the Dutch William of Orange, or William III, invaded with 500 ships and 20,000 soldiers and after some skirmishes forced James II to flee to exile in France, with profound consequences for the religion, constitution and monarchy of England and later Great Britain.

Jones is not alone in forgetting, or misunderstanding, what happened in 1688. In an editorial (28 August), you quoted Nigel Farage as saying, in 2014, that the Bayeux tapestry depicted “the last time we were invaded and taken over”). Let’s hope such ignorance is not widespread and that the loan of the Bayeux tapestry leads to a revival of interest in the study and teaching of history. Richard RossLondon

Spyware can easily fall into the wrong hands – investors should take note

The Guardian Wed, 09 Sep 2026 17:01:10 GMT

The reported targeting of student activists in Serbia is an example of increased misuse, with serious consequences for the commercial spyware industry

The targeting of Serbian activists with advanced spyware (Report, 4 September) is the latest warning in a mounting record of abuse that makes the systemic and foreseeable risks of the commercial spyware industry increasingly impossible to ignore. Investors who aren’t paying attention are leaving their portfolios exposed to growing financial, reputational and human rights risks.

Despite industry assurances that its technology is intended only for investigating terrorists and criminals, spyware has repeatedly been linked to the targeting of journalists, activists, elected officials, opposition leaders, lawyers, judges, academics and civil society. The fallout for the companies involved has been serious: costly litigation, criminal complaints, crippling sanctions, judicial investigations, tightening export restrictions, executives being convicted, severe reputational damage and, in some cases, financial collapse.

That’s before accounting for the damage spyware can inflict elsewhere in an investor’s portfolio. Companies more profitable than spyware firms are forced to defend against attacks, respond to breaches and protect their users and commercially sensitive information. Funding spyware often means funding an attack on their far more valuable portfolio companies.

Investors shouldn’t wait for the next scandal to discover their exposure. They should screen commercial spyware companies from their investment universe, require fund managers to identify and prevent exposure across investment chains, and urge portfolio companies to take action to prevent spyware proliferation.

This is particularly important for development finance institutions, pension funds and other responsible investors whose mandates and reputations rest on creating long-term social value. Financing companies whose products can be used to silence journalists, intimidate civil society and undermine democratic institutions creates risks that extend far beyond any single investment.

The Serbian case should prompt investors to question whether their firm is exposed to commercial spyware. And citizens should be asking, are my tax dollars or pension savings funding this?Meredith Veit Technology and human rights researcher, Business and Human Rights Centre

‘Mr Congeniality’ Burnham advises Badenoch to ditch the point-scoring on defence

The Guardian Wed, 09 Sep 2026 16:59:50 GMT

Leader of the opposition rehashes last week’s questions as she comes up short against a PM who preaches consensus politics

The case of the dog that didn’t bark in the night. Sometimes prime minister’s questions are as notable for the topics that the leader of the opposition doesn’t ask about as for the ones she does. So you have to assume Kemi Badenoch now realises she was on the wrong side of public opinion on the weekend’s protests and the government’s decision to impose sanctions on Israeli illegal settlements.

I guess it’s hard to be too vocal when you fundamentally agree with the rioters. And maybe she has noticed that many of her own party are a little queasy about Palestinian land being seized and people being killed. And no reaction from the US about the sanctions.

Instead, Kemi chose to rehash last week’s questions on defence. It didn’t end well then, and it didn’t end well now. Rather, it exposed Kemi’s fundamental limitations. She appears to have been blindsided by Andy Burnham’s self-invention as Mr Reasonable. The man who listens to the questions and attempts to give an honest answer. Often at great length. The man who repeatedly asks her to step back from point-scoring and invites her to work with him.

This is a problem for the Conservative leader. Not only does she have an inability to work with anyone, her whole shtick is point-scoring. She lives for division. Against Keir Starmer this didn’t seem to matter so much, but Burnham’s more open affability exposes her as an opportunist.

She has no real investment in the questions she asks. They are only a means to an end. A chance to expose some weakness in the government. Kemi isn’t really bothered if people go homeless or we don’t spend 3% of GDP on defence as she is going to be OK either way. In fact she would rather the country fell apart as she has more chance of getting into Downing Street that way. Bring it on. She hadn’t gone in to politics to problem solve. Her goal was her own career development.

Burnham had started the session by mentioning that Friday would mark the 25th anniversary of 9/11. A turning point in global history. Though not apparently for Kemi. Let’s try to be generous. She was only 21 at the time and even more solipsistic than she is now. So perhaps she has never heard of it. Just a little difficulty local to NYC.

Either way, Kemi didn’t feel the need to add any condolences of her own to the families affected. Many of whom were British. She also missed out on her chance to congratulate Donald Trump for his efforts. In recent days, the US president has taken to reimagining himself as one of the great heroes of the terrorist attack. A man who rose from the ashes of the twin towers. Even though he wasn’t there. I still find it amazing that Trump’s fantasies are so readily indulged. No one seems that bothered by his lies. Maybe it’s the true American dream. Anyone can be whatever they want to be.

You had to assume Kemi was focused on defence mainly because she couldn’t come up with anything else. So what we got was the leader of the opposition on repeat. Living in her own echo chamber. Could the government get to 3% of GDP by 2030? Andy looked vaguely surprised to have time travelled back a week and he clearly didn’t have any of the answers in his folder. A couple of times he searched in vain for something new to say, before getting thoroughly pissed off and chucking the folder on the floor.

So the old answers would have to do. Read my lips. It was a bit of a cheek for the Tories to complain about defence when they had repeatedly hollowed out the budget but he would give it a go. The chancellor had been picked precisely because he could be trusted to deliver 3.5% by 2035. But the government wouldn’t be doing a trade off between national security and social security. The Tories’ plan to cut housing benefits by £4bn to fund defence were brain dead as they would only be adding to the number of homeless people for whom councils would have to provide accommodation.

Burnham would not compromise on either national security or essential welfare budgets. The money would come from elsewhere. But the Tories would have to be patient and wait for both the budget and the strategic defence review. That’s if we had that long. There had just been a report that AI might wipe out humanity inside 10 years. Run for the hills everyone.

Perhaps Kemi could try yoga or get a massage to help her chill out in the meantime. But she was too far gone for that. The more affable, the more consensual – “we can do this together, Kemi. Honest” – Mr Congeniality became, the more Kemi looked like she was on the point of losing it. She can bear anything but kindness.

Come the final question and Kemi’s immense surprise that a billionaire had chosen to seek out a tax haven – who would have believed such a thing? – Burnham had the floor to himself. Kemi had teed things up by both accusing him of being a new government and a continuation of the old one –er … make your mind up – which gave him the space to emphasise the difference between himself and Starmer.

This was the moment Andy had been waiting for all morning. What he had come prepared for. If you’re going to be picky, then it was also a bit self-righteous. There again, how often does a prime minister get to be on the right side of history. His chance to say that imposing sanctions on Israeli settlements had been the moral choice. It was only right to expect higher standards of your friends than your enemies. You don’t give your mates a free pass to kill people. To back him up, it wasn’t just most of the Tory party who were with him. It was France, Canada and nine other countries.

There was one more thing that didn’t get a mention. That was Reform’s local difficulties with the Met widening an investigation into its party funding. This was yet another break from Starmer. Keir always used to make a point of calling out Reform and Nige and co used to love the attention. Burnham’s approach has been to freeze Reform out. To ignore them completely. And it seems to be working so far. To be ignored is a fate worse than death.

Trump’s top six falsehoods about 9/11 as 25th anniversary nears

The Guardian Wed, 09 Sep 2026 16:44:53 GMT

US president often brings up al-Qaida attack that struck his home town New York City almost 25 years ago

Donald Trump often brings up September 11, the devastating al-Qaida attack that struck his home town New York City almost 25 years ago.

His recollections of that day have repeatedly included exaggerations and falsehoods – including this week, when he shared an anecdote at a White House event commemorating the attacks that appears to be untrue.

Here are some of the ways Trump has stretched the truth about September 11, beginning shortly after the attacks and continuing into his second presidential term:

Not long after the attacks, Trump said in a telephone interview with a local news anchor that the destruction of the World Trade Center – previously New York City’s tallest building – meant his 40 Wall Street property was now the tallest in downtown Manhattan.

“I mean, 40 Wall Street actually was the second-tallest building in downtown Manhattan. And it was actually before the World Trade Center was the tallest,” Trump claimed. “And then when they built the World Trade Center, it became known as the second tallest. And now it’s the tallest.”

It was not: 70 Pine Street, about a block away, held that distinction.

Trump has repeatedly claimed to have assisted with the recovery from the World Trade Center’s collapse. “Everyone who helped clear the rubble, and I was there, and I watched, and I helped a little bit,” he said at a campaign stop in 2016.

That comment was a rehash of one he made shortly after the attack, where he told a German broadcaster that “we’ll have a couple hundred people down here” helping with the cleanup.

In 2019, PolitiFact interviewed a New York City fire department battalion chief who did not recall Trump sending any workers to the site.

When he first campaigned for the presidency in 2016, Trump repeated a story that “thousands and thousands” of Muslim Americans “were cheering” in Jersey City, New Jersey, on the day of the attacks in 2001.

Despite many fact checks, no evidence has been discovered to back up this claim.

In September 2019, Trump retweeted a video that purported to show the Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar, a Muslim and the first Somali American to serve in the US Congress, dancing on the anniversary of the attacks, calling her: “The new face of the Democrat Party!”

CBS News reported that Omar had been dancing at an event organized by the congressional Black caucus, which was not held on September 11.

In his 2000 book, The America We Deserve, Trump mentioned the al-Qaida leader Osama bin Laden as among “a bewildering series of smaller crises” faced by the US.

At the time, Bin Laden was known to Americans because al-Qaida had in 1998 orchestrated the bombings of US embassies in Kenya and Tanzania.

That didn’t stop Trump from in 2018 writing on X that the US “should have captured Osama Bin Laden long before we did”, adding: “I pointed him out in my book just BEFORE the attack on the World Trade Center.”

During a ceremony at the White House ellipse on Tuesday to honor emergency workers who responded to the attacks, Trump said that when he and a group of workers went to visit lower Manhattan shortly after the attacks, he was carried out by firefighters worried that the lower Manhattan skyscraper One Liberty Plaza – formerly known as the US Steel Building – would collapse.

“Two firemen, big strong guys – and I’m not the smallest guy in the world – they grabbed me under the arm, said: ‘Got to get out of here.’ And they literally lifted me up,” the president claimed. “This is not easy to do – I’m big. They lifted me up and they started running with me. I said: ‘Fellas, I can run myself,’ but they were amazing. But they thought it was coming down. It didn’t come down.”

PolitiFact notes that Trump has told a version of this story before, including in an interview with Fox News that aired earlier this week. It appears to be a stretch.

While concerns about One Liberty Plaza’s stability did prompt the evacuation of at least one nearby building the day after the attack, there’s no evidence Trump was present, while his claim of bringing workers to the site is unsupported.

In the run-up to the festival, the film’s inclusion in the lineup was heavily criticised by the Ukrainian ministry of foreign affairs, in part over the fact that Athens-born Currentzis continues to live and work in Russia, and has never publicly denounced Putin’s war.

“It’s his choice,” Khrzhanovsky said at a press conference on the Lido. “But I think everyone is paying for his own choice, his own life, his own destiny,” added the film-maker, who has renounced his Russian citizenship over the full-scale invasion and lives in exile in Germany.

He referred to his film, in which Currentzis’s character Landau is put under pressure to work on the development of the nuclear bomb and eventually reluctantly agrees. “As you can see in the movie, the main character is also making different choices, and he’s paying for his choices.”

Currentzis did not attend the Venice premiere due to a “last-minute emergency”, but Khzhanovsky said he was still in touch with his lead actor and that he was “one of the greatest conductors of our time”.

Asked about his own position on the state of the war in Ukraine, Khrzhanovsky said: “The only thing I can wish for is peace and success for the Ukrainian government to succeed in the best possible way, to save the country and to win this war.”

DAU was a highly controversial project long before Russian tanks started rolling on to Ukrainian soil. Originally pitched to producers in 2006 as a conventional biopic, and shot between 2008 and 2011 in Kharkiv, Ukraine, the film grew into a gargantuan piece of experimental performance art, with 400 principal roles and approximately 10,000 extras. Some critics have likened it to a “Stalinist Truman Show”.

The death of the dining room: how mealtimes moved to the kitchen – or the sofa

The Guardian Wed, 09 Sep 2026 16:18:20 GMT

The idea of a room that you use only occasionally for sit-down meals has gone out of fashion. Now people have found better ways to use the space

Name: Dining rooms.

Age: Ancient Romans took meals in a room called a triclinium.

Appearance: A room with a big table in the middle, surrounded by chairs.

You mean a kitchen? No, a kitchen has a fridge and an oven. This doesn’t.

Like a conference room in an office? A little, but this room is in your house and it’s just for eating in.

What am I, royalty? Hardly. The dining room was a standard feature of a typical middle-class home.

When was all this? From Victorian times until quite recently.

Why did they decide they needed special dining rooms? Once upon a time, homes tended to have a single, all-purpose entertainment space, but as furnishings in the living room became more elaborate and upholstered, it was thought desirable to designate a separate space for eating.

I guess that makes sense. By the 20th century, dining rooms – once the preserve of the rich – were part of the architecture even in modest homes.

In that case, where did they all go? Most of them have been turned into something else. According to research by insurance provider Aviva, nearly a quarter of homeowners have repurposed their dining rooms.

Into what, exactly? Sometimes, people knock down a wall to make a bigger living room or a bigger kitchen. Others turn dining rooms into gyms or home offices.

Or panic rooms? Possibly. However personal the change, few people feel the need to maintain a separate room just to eat in occasionally.

And they don’t miss their dining rooms? The fashion for bigger kitchens has moved the social focus of mealtimes. These days, people tend to cook and eat their food in the same space.

Really? I eat in front of my computer, on the sofa. In many ways we’ve come full circle: back to spilling food on upholstery.

I don’t think I’ve ever seen a regular house with a dining room. That’s because the shift started some time ago. In 2008, it was predicted that the dining room would be extinct by 2020. According to a study from the time, more than half a million homeowners had plans to renovate by knocking through their dining room in the following 12 months.

And all that knocking through just carried on. Indeed. The vogue for open-plan living has all but obliterated the very idea of rooms.

Do say: “As our lives and ways of interacting change, so the interiors of our homes change with them.”

Don’t say: “This used to be the dining room, but now it’s where three of my nine housemates sleep.”

The Guardian Wed, 09 Sep 2026 16:18:14 GMT

Oil price rises above $100 a barrel as Tehran responds to US attacks that sunk five Iranian tankers

Tehran has said it attacked 10 ships around the strait of Hormuz after the US sunk five Iranian tankers, as escalating strikes between the two countries sent the oil price above $100 a barrel for the first time since July.

The attacks were the sharpest flare-up of strikes in weeks, as the two sides struggled to break a deadlock in the six-month-long war. Fighting in recent weeks has largely revolved around who controls the strait of Hormuz, as Iran attempts to close off the waterway and Washington enforces a blockade of Iranian ports.

The strait is a critical route for global energy supplies, with up to 20% of the world’s oil and gas transiting it before the US-Iran war. The rising price of oil, above the psychologically significant $100 mark, is likely to raise inflation and the price of goods.

Stocks fell on Wall Street while rising fuel and food prices in the US will further frustrate the Trump administration, which faces a midterm election with an unpopular war and a cost-of-living crisis.

Among the vessels struck by Iran were two US vessels and eight oil tankers, the Iranian’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Wednesday.

The IRGC said the 10 vessels were “noncompliant” – a likely reference to ships that tried to traverse the waterway without its permission. At least one sailor was killed and another was missing.

The US denied that its vessels were hit, with US Central Command saying on social media that all “attempted attacks failed”.

A tanker in Iraqi waters carrying 2mi barrels of fuel oil was also struck by a drone, according to Iraqi officials. There were no reports of casualties among the crew and the Iraqi government said there were no reported oil leaks.

Iran said it also fired missiles at US bases in Jordan – 18 of which authorities said were intercepted while two fell in unpopulated areas.

The US had said it destroyed five Iranian oil tankers overnight, publishing videos of ships on fire. The US military said the attacks were a response to Iran targeting a US navy warship twice in the previous two days.

Iranian state TV said the US strikes had followed a “complex intelligence and operational action at dawn” to seize a US underwater drone in the strait. The US said the seized craft was a “defective” older model that did not carry any sensitive data.

The back-and-forth strikes signalled an intensifying escalation between the two sides as Washington announced a new policy of attacking Iranian tankers if Iran targets its warships.

“Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, told reporters.

Iran said it would also escalate its attacks, and that for every two or three tankers struck it would respond by hitting 20. The IRGC said it would also release maps of a new, much-larger area near the strait that it considers forbidden for ships to traverse, extending as far as the Gulf off Chabahar for the first time.

The conflict has also taken on an increasingly regional dimension as the Iran-aligned Houthi movement in Yemen traded strikes with Saudi Arabia.

The Houthis launched a wave of attacks on four cities in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, causing large fires at oil installations and wounding 73 people. The Houthis said dozens of people have been killed in Saudi airstrikes, something unconfirmed by Riyadh.

Fighting re-ignited between the two sides after the Houthis launched an offensive against the Saudi-backed government of Yemen in south Yemen last week, aimed at reaching the Red Sea.

The group is trying to enforce a Red Sea blockade against Saudi Arabia, announced in July. If enforced, it would cut off another route for the kingdom to export its oil.

The Guardian Wed, 09 Sep 2026 16:00:03 GMT

As weight loss drugs have risen all around the world, it has reshaped users’ relationships for better and for worse

As GLP-1 use continues to rise in the US and the UK, people’s bodies are being reshaped – as are their relationships.

“Relationships tend to develop a sense of equilibrium and predictability over time,” says Dr Lindsey Berisha, a licensed clinical psychologist who has worked with clients using GLP-1s for over 10 years. “When one partner undergoes a significant change, it can shift that equilibrium, and even positive change can create uncertainty for both partners.”

Berisha says that her clients who use GLP-1s often report feeling relieved that they are no longer consumed with thoughts of food. These users often develop more self-compassion, she says, as they realize what they previously interpreted as a failure or lack of self-control was a legitimate biological drive and food preoccupation that made life harder for them. “This shift can often be more impactful than the weight loss itself,” she says.

But these changes can elicit mixed reactions from partners, family and friends, says psychologist Dr Rachel Goldman, ranging “from being supportive to feeling insecure, left behind, or worried that the relationship itself is changing”.

None of these reactions mean there is a problem with the medication or the relationship, Goldman emphasizes: “The goal is to recognize those shifts, communicate about them, and find new ways to connect rather than assuming the other person knows what you’re experiencing.”

Below, 11 Guardian readers share how GLP-1 use has shaped their relationships.

My husband is unsupportive. He’s afraid of long-term, currently unknown side-effects and likens GLP-1s to Fen-phen. As a result, I don’t discuss my experience with him. This has been a life-changing drug so far, and I can’t share it with the person I’m closest with. I can’t share the wins, the way I’m amazed and thrilled with how I feel, and I certainly can’t share any concerns or worries. It’s contributed to a distance between us.

I’ve struggled with obesity for my entire adult life, and my family and personal health history put me at very high risk of dying young due to complications from the disease. Brennan’s victory puts him in a small bracket of riders, including Tadej Pogacar – who was overwhelming favourite to win this year’s Vuelta before he suffered a season-ending injury in a crash in stage eight – to claim five or more stages at a single Grand Tour.

Jamaica’s plea to the king: use your authority to ensure colonial slavery is examined

The Guardian Wed, 09 Sep 2026 15:44:11 GMT

The UK drew immense wealth from our country. But was the slavery that underpinned the empire ever lawful? We deserve a fair hearing

Jamaican delegates arrive in UK to hand slavery reparations petition to King Charles

On 6 September 1781, the Zong slave ship set out on the final leg of its voyage to Black River, Jamaica. Four hundred and forty two enslaved Africans were on board – twice the number of people the ship could safely accommodate.

Twelve weeks later, 132 enslaved people were murdered by the ship’s crew by being pushed overboard to their deaths. The crew’s justification was the ship had insufficient water supplies to keep everyone alive for the rest of the voyage – a claim later proved false in the British courts.

This event, and the legal case that followed, added significant weight to the abolitionist movement in the UK, as did uprisings throughout the Caribbean led by the enslaved.

My ancestors achieved their emancipation in 1834, more than 50 years on from the horrors of the Zong. It took a further 128 years for Jamaicans to achieve our independence, on 6 August 1962.

At that time, Jamaica ceased to be a British colony. But the legacies of our colonial past linger, not least because we remain a member of the Commonwealth, with King Charles as our head of state.

The consequences of the slave trade reverberate deeply to this day. The UK drew immense wealth from Jamaica during the colonial era, but centuries of exploitation left us with an economic and social deficit we are still fighting to overcome.

Our natural resources were ravaged during the colonial period, leaving us one of the most vulnerable regions in the world in relation to the climate crisis and extreme weather events.

Our infrastructure is massively underdeveloped; our most talented young people often choose to immigrate to the US or come here to the UK. Poverty levels remain high; educational disadvantage persists; health outcomes are poor – all of this can be directly linked to our history of enslavement and colonialism.

While the government of Jamaica works tirelessly to address the economic and social deficits, legacy issues persist.

Here in the UK, meanwhile, hundreds of thousands of people have African-Caribbean heritage.

It is against this backdrop that we have, this week, filed a petition with King Charles, asking him to refer three specific questions on transatlantic chattel enslavement to the judicial committee of the privy council. The questions focus on whether enslavement in Jamaica was ever lawful and whether there is an obligation on the UK to provide some form of reparatory remedy.

It is important to stress we are not asking King Charles to answer these questions himself. Rather, the people of Jamaica are asking him, as our head of state, to allow our case to have a fair hearing in the British courts.

Drawing on the Judicial Committee Act of 1833 – which confers a special power on King Charles to refer questions of legal and constitutional importance to the judicial committee – this is the first time any Commonwealth state has pursued this legal route for the cause of reparatory justice. It is, in fact, such a rarely used legal route that it took us some time – with both the palace and the privy council – to confirm the exact process for filing the petition correctly.

In pursuing this route, we are placing our faith in the British legal system, one of the longest-established in the world.

We are seeking a chance to put forward the legal argument for reparations – and our legal case coincides with growing political and public momentum on this issue.

Sign up to Cotton Capital

Starting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the world

after newsletter promotion

In March, the UN passed a motion, recognising enslavement as “the gravest crime against humanity”. In May, Pope Leo XIV made a historic apology for the Vatican’s role in legitimising enslavement.

In June, heads of state, policymakers and activists from more than 80 countries (including some former European colonial powers) gathered in Ghana for the Accra Reparatory Justice Conference. A Global Advisory Council on Reparatory Justice was established after the event, of which our own prime minister, Dr Andrew Holness, is a member.

Just last week, the UN committee on the elimination of racial discrimination (CERD) issued guidance stating countries were legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and to take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial ​discrimination.

Now, through our petition, Jamaica is adding our own distinct effort to the global campaign for reparatory justice, aiming to test the legal principles of relevance to this issue.

Our petition has been endorsed by the heads of government of all Caricom countries, while Ghana’s president, John Dramani Mahama, has also expressed his strong support.

King Charles has previously expressed deep personal sorrow about the history of enslavement. He has the constitutional power and the personal moral authority to allow this question to now be legally examined. Two hundred and forty-five years on from the Zong massacre, we are asking him to grant this request.

Olivia Grange is the Jamaican government’s minister for culture, gender, entertainment and sport

I want to change my face. I’m not talking cosmetic surgery, although if chubby cheeks could be surgically de-chubbed I’d have to consider it. Surgery can’t help me – if only it were that simple. What I seek to change is the expression on my face, my whole disposition, the face I present to the world. Mine’s all wrong, insomuch as I look as if there’s something wrong. Very often I’ll be asked what the matter is.

“Nothing,” I say.

“Sure?”

“Yes, why do you ask?”

“Well, you just look miserable.”

Point taken. Very often, when I tell a friend that all is good with me, they ask if I’ve thought about telling that to my face.

Well, now I am – I am telling my face to cheer up. I don’t know how or when it got stuck this way. It’s been at least 13 years. I know this because back then something was written in the Daily Mirror which second-mentioned me as “the gloomy 46-year-old”. Not angry, or sad, or scornful. Just gloomy. Tragic, really. And now I’m the gloomy 59-year-old.

Last month I saw this bloke in a cafe in Trieste. So entranced was I at the sunniness of his disposition that I couldn’t take my eyes off him. It wasn’t just the faintest of smiles on his lips, it was the kindness in his eyes and the aura of quiet contentment. It wasn’t some smug satisfaction with his own circumstances so much as contentment with the world as a whole. He radiated the conviction that everything and everyone was just fine. It was infectious. That cafe, the square, the city, all felt afloat on a sea of gladness. It was that profound. A rising tide of serenity raises all boats.

He didn’t betray any alarm even as he registered me, this gloomy stranger, staring at him in wonder. He merely widened his eyes a little and gave an almost imperceptible nod in acknowledgment of the happy fact that life could be worse.

I want to be him instead of his opposite, exuding bleakness. It’s high time – I will be 60 next year. My seventh decade will be my cheery era. Who says you can’t teach an old dog new tricks? It just takes longer than you might hope. After a lifetime of defaulting to an upside-down smile, a resting happy face is not something you can paint on just because you like the cut of a stranger’s jib in a cafe in Trieste. I discovered this there and then when I tried a big grin on for size; it didn’t fit. Even Happy Man looked unsettled.

When you smile, the world smiles back. Not at me it doesn’t. Try as I might, I can’t smile right. Yes, I smile nicely if I bump into someone I like, or my team score a goal, or someone says something amusing – but getting a default, not-thinking-about-it, resting happy face is quite beyond me. I think it’s all the thinking about it. Out for a walk, if I was thinking non-stop about walking, I’d soon be tripping over my feet. So it is with smiling. My lips and cheeks are all over the shop, while my facial muscles are in constant motion in search of a natural smile they can live with.

I can’t settle on anything suitable. Smiling the wrong smile, especially at women, feels a bit forward; smiling at blokes might even invite a fight. WTF are you grinning at, mate? I’m spooking people. And, clocking my reflection in a shop window, I spook myself. How do I find the face I want? A survey perhaps – “Excuse me, madam, may I ask what my facial expression is conveying?” In the meantime, I’ll practise into a mirror seeking a countenance suggesting mildness, tolerance, hope, openness. Anything but gloom.

Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

Norway has observed a minute’s silence as it takes leave of King Harald V in a series of ceremonies, bringing to a close 13 days of ​national mourning that followed the popular monarch’s death last month at the age of 89.

Tens of thousands of people lined the streets of Oslo and foreign heads of state and government converged on the Norwegian capital for the funeral of the late king, a light-touch and unassuming reformer who ruled for more than three decades.

With the king’s casket carried on an artillery carriage, draped in Norway’s red royal banner and topped with white flowers, the funeral cortege made its way on foot along Oslo’s main avenue from royal palace to the cathedral, as a 21-gun salute rang out from the Akershus fortress.

King Haakon VIII, who succeeded his father on Harald’s death, and other royal family members walked in the cortege, with Harald’s widow, Queen Sonja, 89, and Haakon’s wife, Queen Mette-Marit, who is recovering from a lung transplant in June, following in a car.

The procession was followed by a church ceremony attended by royals including Britain’s Prince William and Princess Anne; Spain’s King Felipe and Queen Letizia; ‌Sweden’s royal family; Denmark’s King Frederik and Queen Mary; the Netherlands’ King Willem-Alexander and Queen Maxima; and Japan’s Crown Prince Akishino.

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and political leaders and dignitaries from more than 20 countries were at the service, at which the speaker of Norway’s parliament, Masud Gharahkhani, recalled a monarch who was “not afraid to meet his people with his rubber boots on”.

The prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, said Harald “struck a balance between being stately and being down-to-earth. He made Norway greater. He spoke of a ‘we’ in Norway where everyone is there for each other.”

After the service four F-35 fighter jets flew over the cathedral, one breaking away to symbolise the king’s passing. The casket was then carried to the Akershus fortress where it was due to be lowered into the royal crypt, next to Harald’s parents and grandparents, in a private ceremony.

Norwegian police said securing the funeral had been the largest planned operation in the force’s history. More than 46,000 Norwegians have filed past the king’s casket in the past week and schoolchildren were allowed to miss ⁠classes for the occasion.

‘I’m not a robot’: Josh Kerr primed to peak against arch rival Ingebrigtsen

The Guardian Wed, 09 Sep 2026 15:00:04 GMT

A $150,000 prize in Budapest has the record-breaking Scot buzzing but the middle-distance star insists he’s no longer chasing paydays

The richest event in track and field history launches in Budapest this weekend, and the prospect of walking away with $150,000 at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship has got Josh Kerr ready to rumble again, on and off the track.

Some critics have noted that the Scot has run only five times in 2026 – compared with Amy Hunt’s 43 races – and has had to rely on a wild card from World Athletics to even compete in Budapest.

Others, including the double Olympic champion Jakob Ingebrigtsen, have questioned why Kerr swerved the chance to race in front of his home fans at the European championships in Birmingham last month.

Kerr’s response? To insist that “I’m not a robot”, before pointing out that in four of his five races this year he has broken the world mile record, set a personal best over 800m, and won gold at the world indoor championships over 3,000m and the Commonwealth Games over 1500m.

“I’m tired of just saying it,” he says. “I’m a human being at the end of the day. And to run a world indoor championships and come out with a gold medal there, go after a PB over 800m, which I was able to do for the first time in seven years, get a Commonwealth Games gold medal, and and also go get a a world record, and then go after an outdoor major championships, that’s enough for me. I’m not a robot.

“The first question I was asked after running the mile world record is: ‘When are you going to go after the 1500m world record?’ And it’s just not that simple to peak like we did for London, and then to reset for the Commonwealth Games, and then reset again for a world record attempt, and then reset again for Europeans, and then reset again for Ultimates.”

Kerr has not been seen on a track since competing in Glasgow in early August, which has meant missing out on paydays and a chance to further promote his sport. But the 28-year-old athlete insists he deliberately targets “two to four big dates a year” and wants to race only when he is in prime shape.

“I’m not trying to avoid racing. I love racing. I just don’t love racing when I’m not ready to go. And the reason I can race so well is because I pick my races. These next three years are going to be some of the biggest in my career. So I’m not going to get greedy.

“If you race a bunch, you’re going to have long-term injury problems, if you want to have a career that’s 10 or 12 years long, then you can’t do that. I’ve been caught chasing paydays early on in my career, and it doesn’t end up with long-term success.”

However, Kerr is excited by the Ultimate Championship, a new three-day competition which effectively serves as a mini world championships. The event, which has a $10m prize fund, is also being used as a testing ground for innovations in the sport, including a black infield, athletes being allowed to make content, and a more party-style atmosphere, all designed to attract a younger audience.

“I think it would be a lot more of an off-year, or a dud year, without a championship that we can all attend in September,” Kerr says. “Packing out stadiums, putting on a championship that people enjoy, and pushing the marketing on it. There’s only really one step left of how the sport gets bigger, and I think it’s sports betting.”

Kerr is in no doubt who his money will be on if he ends up racing his nemesis Ingebrigtsen, who is scheduled to compete in the 5,000m on Friday and then against the Scot in the 1500m final on Sunday.

“I’m very happy that he’s back running and racing,” Kerr says. “I think it’s great. He’s one of the best 1500m and 5k runners of all time, and I’m excited to go out and race him. I’m not going to lose, but I’m excited to go out there and race.”

Kerr is also excited about athletics being able to capitalise on the global running boom, and says the improved prize money is another sign that the sport is heading in the right direction. “We’re seeing progress, I’m not going to complain about progress,” he says.

“Obviously, $150,000 is is a lot of money. It’s not as much as other big sports, but they’ve earned that through years and years of continuing to push into marketing, and we’re moving in the right direction with these championships, and so I can’t complain.”

As Kerr points out, it’s also harder for lots of athletes to make money because there are so many events. “In tennis, there’s one winner,” he says. “In track and field, there’s 25 winners. But races and contracts are doing a lot better than they’ve ever been. Running is going through a boom, and we’re seeing that in shoe sales, on the athlete side, as well as social media.”

Meanwhile, returning to Budapest brings back happy memories for Kerr, given it was where he won his first world title in 2023. “It was an incredibly pivotal day for me. Your first world title is the most special. I just hadn’t really won a lot. And it was starting to really piss me off.”

While Kerr faces a strong field that includes the Olympic champion Cole Hocker and the Diamond League final winner Cameron Myers, it is clear he expects to win again. “I’m here to prove that I’m going to be the best 1500m runner of all time or of our generation at least,” he says.

“There are different ways to win a championship. One is to be so dominant that no one else has an option to win. That is what we are going for this year. If you want to make it fast, if you want to make it slow, you are going to be in trouble either way. That’s what Budapest should be for me.”

Seven of my colleagues were killed in Gaza. There and in Ukraine, aid workers are no longer safe

The Guardian Wed, 09 Sep 2026 14:00:01 GMT

It now seems the 2024 attack on World Central Kitchen workers was a deliberate IDF tactic. The protections of the Geneva conventions have become paper thin

José Andrés is the founder of the food aid charity World Central Kitchen

In times of war, the hard and vital work of supplying food, water and medicine has been protected by international agreements for almost 80 years. Yet those protections have been systematically and repeatedly ignored in the two most bloody wars of recent years: Ukraine and Gaza.

Russia has attacked healthcare targets in Ukraine more than 3,200 times since the full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to the World Health Organization: about twice a day on average. That includes many “double-tap” attacks on the same target in quick succession, which are especially lethal for first responders.

In April, the UN security council heard that in the past three years, at least 1,010 humanitarian workers had died in 21 countries. More than half of those were in Gaza and the West Bank. That is three times more than the 377 killed in the previous three years.

“This is not an accidental escalation,” said Tom Fletcher, the UN’s undersecretary-general for humanitarian affairs. “It is the collapse of protection.” This collapse of protection has led directly to the airstrikes on aid workers in Gaza, including seven of my own World Central Kitchen (WCK) team, who were killed by the IDF in April 2024 despite full cooperation and coordination with the military.

At the time, the IDF concluded that the attacks had been “a grave mistake” and a breach of its own standard operating procedures. It stated: “We consider the vital humanitarian activity of international aid organizations to be of utmost importance, and we will continue to work to coordinate and assist their activities, while ensuring their safety and safeguarding their lives.” The reserve colonel who ordered the strikes, Nochi Mendel, was dismissed for his actions.

However, these fine words were undercut by the IDF itself, when its military prosecutor decided last month not to open a criminal investigation into the airstrikes on our convoy. Now we understand, because of a Guardian investigation, that the targeting of the WCK convoy was the result of a military tactic of guilt by association. It means that lethal force can be triggered by suspicions, shadows, or simply prejudice. This undefined, unjustified and unlawful tactic is a mortal threat to all humanitarians. What are the protections under these conditions?

It is worth remembering why the fourth Geneva convention was created in 1949 and embraced by the world, with the express intention of protecting civilians in war and meeting basic humanitarian needs. In the immediate aftermath of the second world war, the scale of civilian suffering shocked the world’s conscience. Indeed, one of the key architects of the convention was Georges Cahen-Salvador, a French Jewish civil servant, whose family was imprisoned at the Drancy internment camp. They were being deported to Auschwitz in 1943 when they managed to escape to Switzerland. He was one of several survivors who drafted the fourth convention.

The convention’s assertions of shared values in war are not lost today, but they are struggling to survive.

David Ben-Gurion, Israel’s founding father, famously said: “The fate of Israel depends on two things: its strength and its righteousness.” It’s something that Israel’s military leaders like to quote, but their record falls far short. Humanitarian values are the foundation of righteousness; they are what separate responsible nation states from terrorist groups or rogue states who don’t care about civilian suffering. The protection of aid workers allows the world to ensure that civilians are cared for.

AI could kill all humans in next decade, warn experts: but how seriously should we take them?

The Guardian Wed, 09 Sep 2026 13:46:44 GMT

Alarming warnings from industry insiders increase pressure for curbs on artificial superintelligence

Does artificial superintelligence really pose a risk greater than nuclear weapons? Is there a significant chance of “a Chornobyl-sized catastrophe”. Might there even be a greater than 10% chance that AI could “kill all humans” in the next decade?

These warnings were issued over the past 48 hours on both sides of the Atlantic about the potential impact of a technology that most people still think of as a more talkative search engine.

Some of the threats were raised in the UK as MPs and peers began to wrestle with the danger of AI outperforming human capabilities. The nuclear warnings came from Des Browne, a former defence secretary, and Prof Stuart Russell, an eminent Berkeley computer scientist.

Beatrice Fihn, who won the 2017 Nobel peace prize for leading the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons, told parliamentarians: “It is not the first time we’re confronted with abilities that could end up killing us all.”

The session on Monday was convened by Control AI, a lobbying group pushing for international regulation of the technology. It is backing a bill tabled in parliament this week by the Labour MP Alex Sobel and aimed at banning the creation of artificial superintelligence (ASI).

On Tuesday night, a senior employee at Anthropic admitted he believed there was a greater than 10% chance the technology could “kill all humans” in the next decade and warned that his AI company did not have a plan to ensure ASI was aligned, meaning it did no harm. Predictions for when ASI might be reached vary from several years to more than a decade.

Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, posted the comment after Jacob Coxon, a 28-year-old researcher at the San Francisco company and previously at OpenAI, resigned, claiming “neither company was acting responsibly”. He said they were “gambling with our lives”.

Coxon said the risks at Anthropic were well understood but they were “locked in a race to get there first”. In a glimmer of hope, he added that he was optimistic about the potential for coordination between US labs on pacing their progress in the race.

Anthropic has been approached for comment on the issue. OpenAI pointed to a statement from its chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, who said last week: “International coordination on future AI development needs to become a top priority for governments around the world.”

The push for wider coordination to control ASI was at the heart of events at Westminster this week. According to the Financial Times, government officials voiced concern that Anthropic had declined to submit its latest model – Mythos 5.1 – to the UK’s AI Security Institute for pre-release testing.

Only a few US organisations have had access to Mythos 5.1, the Cabinet Office confirmed. A spokesperson added: “The AI Security Institute continues to collaborate closely with industry partners, including Anthropic.”

The Labour MP Darren Jones has written to the prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the heads of the UN and the OECD calling for a “multinational treaty for the regulated and safe development of superintelligence – not a ban on innovation or scientific endeavour but a safety-first approach to the rapid development of this technology”.

Citing Coxon’s resignation, Jones added: “The debate ranges from the end of humanity to claims of ‘marketing hype’. Either way, governments must now step in.”

On the other side of the Atlantic, Bernie Sanders ratcheted up his AI safety campaign this week by again calling on Congress to regulate the technology. He pointed to polling suggesting that 81% of Americans believed their politicians should take action.

The independent senator for Vermont said: “We can’t allow a handful of greedy people to play God and determine the future of humanity – our economy, environment, democracy, privacy and more – without public input.”

Sign up to TechScape

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

ControlAI is funded by Jaan Tallinn, the multi-billionaire founder of Skype who calls himself an “anti-extinctionist”. He has dedicated part of his fortune to campaigning for AI safety and says some senior AI executives would be happy for humanity to be wiped out.

Despite being an early investor in Anthropic and Google DeepMind, two of the leading AI labs, Tallinn estimates that 10-15% of AI employees believe the technology will be a worthy successor to humanity.

He said in an interview earlier this summer: “A fairly known AI researcher said to me ‘Jaan, don’t worry about this. Humans are a disposable species’. From what I understand he was fine with becoming extinct.”

Tallinn’s lobby group ran the session for MPs and peers at Westminster on Monday and urged them to back measures to curb the most powerful AI models. On every chair was a copy of the book, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: The Case Against Superintelligent AI.

The politicians heard from Russell, who made the Chornobyl warning and said: “The other possibility is a much larger catastrophe, in which humanity loses control irreversibly. But we have no say over whether we continue to exist.”

Browne said that when he was defence secretary he thought nuclear war was the most likely threat facing humanity. Now he believed “a superintelligent AI poses a threat on the same, possibly, a greater scale”.

Other contributors were more cautious. Dr Andrew Rogoyski, of the Surrey Institute for People-Centred AI, said: “In reality, these systems are nowhere near as versatile as humans, let alone humans acting collectively. I suspect we’re heading towards ‘the great disappointment’ where advanced AI turns out to be too expensive and not useful enough to continue in its current form.”

David Barber, director of Sofair, a state-backed AI research lab combining academics from Oxford, Cambridge, Edinburgh and UCL, said he was worried about people “throwing the baby out with the bathwater”.

“AI is not going to go away,” he said. “It’s incredibly useful, whether or not you allow it in a fully unconstrained way to access the internet and various systems that’s potentially problematic. We may need to learn how to better control these things. There are vulnerabilities in the software frameworks that need to be patched. But that’s doable.

“What we need as a country is to get to grips with the duality that is both an incredibly important and useful technology, and at the same time, it’s something that needs to be carefully thought about and carefully controlled.”

Sandra Wachter, a professor at the Oxford Internet Institute, said she did not believe in “Terminator scenarios” but that AI posed real threats including its environmental impact, spreading of misinformation and replacing jobs.

“These problems are real and urgent and need addressing now,” she said. “Terminator scenarios are a big distraction from real issues.”

Gary Marcus, an AI industry commentator and academic, said: “There is a difference between superintelligence that is aligned (if such a thing is possible) and superintelligence that is not.

“It is at least conceivable that the former might be net positive. So far we have neither, but a superabundance of hype combined with a striking lack of prudence on OpenAI’s part has gotten us where we are, with intense mistrust all around.”

Madgwick said he was at home on Tuesday evening when he was called and told that about 40 people had gathered outside the Marriott hotel, many wearing balaclavas or other face coverings, after reports that asylum seekers were staying there.

He went there and spoke to the hotel manager, who “explained the situation” – the hotel was hosting members of an under-21 cricket team from Pakistan, who are touring the south coast and using the Marriott as their base.

“I also spoke to the coach of the team, who was very understanding,” Madgwick said. “I went out to the protesters and told them, ‘You’ve got it wrong guys, it’s a cricket club.’ They left within a couple of minutes. It was a massively unfortunate incident.

“From the perspective of the people of Portsmouth who are already on high alert, this was a coach from the same company which was turning up with about 40 foreign men.”

Madgwick said he accepted it was far from ideal for a masked group to assemble outside a hotel purely because a group of apparently foreign men had arrived.

He said: “It doesn’t make our city look like the welcoming city it is. But it’s reflective of the climate we live in, and where people are deeply concerned about the issues.”

The news first emerged after Madgwick put out a Facebook post urging people to stay away from the area. He wrote: “There were reports that possible migrants were staying in the Marriott hotel. I can confirm that is NOT the case. Please don’t attend the hotel.

At the hotel, as well as speaking to the hotel staff and team coach, Madgwick was shown “proof” that the men were indeed cricketers, he added. Madgwick said he had subsequently made the post private as it was attracting abusive comments.

Since the incident, the England and Wales Cricket Board has contacted the Pakistan Cricket Board to check on the wellbeing of those involved, and is reviewing security arrangements for the remainder of the squad’s tour.

A final game, also an ODI, is scheduled to be played in Guildford on Saturday. Pakistan’s senior men’s team is also in the country, playing the third and final Test against England at Edgbaston.
