‘I thought a devil was about to appear from the smoke’: Jerry Hsu’s best photograph

The Guardian Wed, 09 Sep 2026 13:35:26 GMT

‘The black cloud emerged from a grate in the street. I guess something underground was on fire. It was hilariously cinematic – just one of those eerie, spontaneous things that happen in a city’

This image was taken in 2011 or 2012, just after I had moved to Los Angeles. I was downtown, an area I don’t go to that much, walking around with my camera. Some black smoke started to emerge from a grate in the street – I guess something underground was on fire. It was hilariously cinematic, as if some sort of devil was going to appear. It was really just one of those eerie, spontaneous things that happen in a city. There is a very powerful feeling of surrender when I am photographing. I have to submit to the authority of ignorance when I’m out there.

I grew up in San Jose, which is a sprawling American suburb – there’s no city about it. I came to LA because I was depressed where I lived, and I had just met my future wife, who didn’t want to live in San Jose either. LA is not really a city, it’s hundreds of places. You can drive 15 minutes and be in a completely different environment – the beach, the mountains. There’s a weird sentience to the city, if you let it take you. I get an inexplicable desire to just get in the car and go.

Despite the fact it’s sunny every day, there is a noir that is pervasive here. I really like the dark part of the city. There’s a transgressive pulse, and if you search hard enough, there’s a lot of intimacy too. In my book How About Never, there are photographs of big things – fires, hard-hitting events – but at the same time, the smaller things. Cities are cruel and I wanted to capture that, but I also found compassion.

After I had done the edit for the book, I looked at it and realised that it was also about my relationship with my wife. The photographs span from the time we met to when our marriage ended earlier this year. My wife is a prominent character in it, although you don’t see her face until the end. It’s a very vulnerable photograph of her in a hospital bed. I have a lot of beautiful photographs of her, but I didn’t choose those. I think that in all relationships, vulnerability is the key to how we truly connect, and that was difficult for us. The book is a fantasy of what I was searching for, a dream about what I wanted it to look like and what it couldn’t be – all of the opposing forces, all the fire, water, destruction – and at the same time, hope and beauty. These are the contradictions you find in a relationship.

I started skateboarding at 12, and at 16 I turned pro. I was a professional for 25 years. I guess the most obvious connection between that and photography is that skateboarders are constantly seeing the environment in a way other people don’t. We see a park bench, a handrail or an embankment and we think about how we can manipulate it for our purposes. There’s a constant searching and endless curiosity, thinking about how to make an environment our own. As a skateboarder, you’re also hardwired to react quickly – you have to reach a flow state and not hesitate to do something that might be life-threatening. It takes a lot of focus to process information quickly – it’s a type of premonition about what’s about to happen. Skateboarding taught me from an early age that I have permission to view reality how I want; to take from it what I want. It gave me the permission I needed to make my own choices, which helped a lot with photography, and in my life generally.

I am interested in dreams, and in my book I treated the city as if it were my subconscious. I wander through it as if I am in a dream. A dream shows you images and is trying to tell you something about yourself. LA was doing that to me, it was showing me all these things I was attracted to, and I was capturing and collecting them without knowing what I was going to do with them.

I have always been painfully shy and interacting with the world is not easy, but this connects me with it and it’s how I can speak about it. Photography is a solitary practice and making work can be so isolating - I was scared to show my work, scared of being rejected or misunderstood, but I wanted to tell this story. People look at this book and think it’s bleak – and sure, it is, but there’s also a lot of hope in it. The last image of a cat, moving out of the frame to the right, is about moving forward and going on living, despite all of this.

How About Never is published by MACK.

Born: San Jose, California 1981High point: My new book, How About Never. Top tip: Always research. Copy artists you are drawn to and your voice will eventually emerge.

Farage is clearly struggling – I saw that for myself. But his legacy will be a poison that runs deep

The Guardian Wed, 09 Sep 2026 13:00:03 GMT

The mood at the Reform conference was volatile and brittle. But the forces massing further to the right of the party are testament to its impact

For much of the time since Nigel Farage resumed the Reform UK leadership two long years ago, his party has been an island of relative stability in the increasingly rough sea of British politics. While other parties plunged queasily in the polls, messily purged dissidents, argued publicly about their direction and changed leaders, Farage dominated Reform UK and gave impregnably self-assured interviews. The party’s popularity moved steadily upwards, comfortably above that of all the others.

It is a paradox that a new party with wildly expectant members, not many experienced politicians and few properly worked-out policies became the pole around which the country’s political debate revolved, and yet this seemed to do no harm to Reform’s chances of winning the next general election. As with rising rightwing populist parties across the world, Reform’s tendency to make it up as it went along appeared to be not a weakness but, for many voters, much of its appeal.

That seems less the case now. Amid multiple, worsening funding scandals, and with the party openly divided about how to respond to them, this year Reform has lost about a quarter of its support and its poll lead over Labour. There are internal mutterings about the attention-seeking and leadership ambitions of its home affairs spokesperson, the relentlessly abrasive Zia Yusuf, and its Treasury spokesperson, the slippery former Tory Robert Jenrick.

Meanwhile, Farage himself, who at 62 is two decades older than them, and has been active in politics for more than 40 years, may be finally losing his composure. Interviewed by the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg last weekend, after months of largely and uncharacteristically avoiding journalists, he switched between anger at his enemies, claims to victimhood and unconvincing insouciance: eyes bulging with fury one moment, head bobbing with forced laughter the next. Even by the feverish standards of modern British politics, it was a strange, almost manic performance.

What might happen to Reform and our wider politics if the party’s troubles continue and deepen? The answers may be less reassuring than Reform’s enemies like to think. While the diminishing likelihood of a Reform government is welcome, the party’s crisis could change Reform, and the forces massing further to the right of it – both in parliament and on the streets – in unpredictable and dangerous ways.

At the party’s conference last week, the mood felt brittle and volatile. Whereas speakers insisted that Reform was still a “government in waiting”, and banners, lanyards and speeches relentlessly hyped its potential “first 100 days”, the delegates I spoke to were worried about the party’s slide in the polls and general election chances, Andy Burnham’s assured start as prime minister, and the growing pressure Farage was under. After his speech was repeatedly interrupted by hecklers from the green group Climate Resistance, I overheard two delegates, mild-looking, middle-aged men in suits, discussing the protest. “It’s got to stop,” said one. The other said: “Smash ’em in the face!”

Another Reform reaction to the party’s difficulties has been to announce ever more extreme, dramatic policies, such as deporting foreign prisoners, possibly to the infamously brutal jails of El Salvador, and deploying the Royal Navy and Royal Marines to intercept and take all small boat migrants back to France, in “the biggest military operation in the English Channel since the second world war”. In his conference speech, Yusuf described “Operation Fortress” with lingering detail, while huge images of a military helicopter and warship were projected on to the set behind him, and a storm of applause came from the packed hall. Perhaps the potential for such authoritarian political theatre and performatively aggressive policy was always there in Reform, but both feel much more central to its activities now.

“All parliamentary recesses will be cancelled,” declared Farage in his speech. “Parliament will sit, if necessary, for 24 hours a day, six days a week, until we pass the necessary legislation.” Nothing would be allowed to obstruct “the will of the people” – even though, with modern election turnouts low and half a dozen parties now competing seriously across the country, a Reform victory might represent the will of only a fifth of voters, or less.

This year, with the party losing the electoral initiative, new movements have appeared on the anti-migrant right: the even more hardline Restore Britain, and Patriot Platform, the black-clad blockaders of Dover and Portsmouth. Though Farage has criticised both groups, the latter for wearing balaclavas at their protests, the boundaries between Reform and these rivals are not as firm as he would like more mainstream rightwing Britons – whose support Reform badly needs – to think. Restore and Reform’s rhetoric and policies can be hard to distinguish, while on Monday, Yusuf visited Portsmouth and spoke amicably with Patriot Platform’s organiser, Daniel Thomas, a convicted attempted kidnapper.

Thomas told Yusuf he was upset by Farage’s criticism, and that the protests were not meant to intimidate, but that he still considered Farage a “hero” for his campaigning against the small boats. “You have done really well,” said Thomas. “A lot of people support you.” “Thank you,” said Yusuf, who listened to him at length, nodding respectfully. Then Yusuf replied: “I will take that message – you’ve got my word … take that back to him [Farage].”

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The encounter suggested that Reform’s problems may create new alliances and opportunities for the hard right, reshaping but not weakening anti-migrant politics. While the Conservative shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, condemned the Portsmouth violence, he added: “People are genuinely angry at the government’s failure to stop the boats.” Even Labour dares not challenge the legitimacy of what the policing minister, Sarah Jones, called on Monday “the frustration we see in our communities today” about the boats. Just as Reform’s rise made both Labour and the Tories more nationalist and socially conservative, there is a danger that its decline, temporary or otherwise, could continue that process, as they compete for its former supporters.

If you’re opposed to Reform’s policies, and especially if you might become one of their victims, then its setbacks this year may be a relief. But that relief will only be partial while its ideas and claims remain so thoroughly embedded across politics and the media, and in many people’s everyday conversations and thinking. One day, Farage will retire, but what he represents will be even harder to stop.

Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

The Uprising review – the peasants are revolting in muddled historical epic

The Guardian Wed, 09 Sep 2026 13:00:02 GMT

Andrew Garfield’s charisma can’t save Paul Greengrass’s grim and depressingly generic period piece

Hollywood loves giving young actors their own historical epic as much as audiences seem to dislike watching them. Timothée Chalamet and Chris Pine’s least remembered roles are in the medieval set films The King and Outlaw King (no relation), Ridley Scott’s The Last Duel made back only a third of its $100m budget and earlier this year, the Saudi-backed seventh-century drama Desert Warrior starring Anthony Mackie and Ben Kingsley quietly became one of the biggest flops of all time. Last week, it was reported that Scott blamed the failure of Gladiator II on Paul Mescal not being “masculine enough” in a logical leap which only makes sense if your barometer for masculinity is a man who throws hotel phones and yells at producers in storage closets.

On paper, The Uprising should be different: it’s a historical epic from a blue-chip director (the Bourne trilogy’s Paul Greengrass), a nuanced, introspective leading man (Andrew Garfield) and a milieu that uncomfortably chimes with the western world’s backslide into repressive authoritarianism (The Peasants’ Revolt of 1381). In reality, it is a disjointed slog through the mud with the emotional depth of a History Channel rerun.

Through Greengrass’s lens, late 14th-century England seems like an utterly wretched place, not only because of the sludge-grey sky, scratchy brown sacks that everyone wears and the fact that no one seems to have had a wash in weeks, but because a despotic king treats the country’s people like scum, gouging them out of what little they have with hefty taxes to advance his own vainglorious agenda. Garfield’s character, who identifies only as Ploughman (“I am what I do,” he grunts), is mourning the loss of his wife and two children after they died from the plague, and will not stand for it any more. When asked for proof of his family’s death, one day he swipes clean the table of the taxman. “We’ve given you enough,” he cries, as the townspeople’s collective rage boils over into a riot.

He’s an unconvincing hero, this gruff Ploughman. The character seems to have been constructed as an everyman figure who unites the common people of England, but without any particular magnetism or spice, he often feels like he could be any man. His troupe soon meets two people who actually were in the Peasants’ Revolt: the priest John Ball and rebel leader Wat Tyler (Jamie Bell and Cosmo Jarvis: both great and, unlike Garfield, both look like they actually could be from the late middle ages). “Join us, Ploughman,” beckons Tyler, as Garfield’s character, his band of brothers and a tomboy named Alyce, Thomasin McKenzie, unite to march on London with an aim to confront the king and restore England to the egalitarian principles of the Domesday Book.

Thus follows a rather hectic-feeling race from one greige setting to the next as the rebels have their run of modern-day Kent, assembling in Maidstone before storming Canterbury cathedral, and then traveling to meet the king and his men in Blackheath. Greengrass’s camerawork can occasionally swoon, with stunning aerial shots of a flotilla on the Thames, but his signature handheld style is a trick that has gone stale: the only uprising I felt during the seasick fight scenes was my breakfast threatening to return on me.

High points briefly come from Katherine Waterston’s satisfyingly icy turn as the king’s mother as well as Tom Hollander and Stephen Dillane as members of the slimy royal counsel, and there is one wickedly gruesome moment in the third act that feels genuinely envelope-pushing. But there are far too many scenes revolving around the Ploughman ominously polishing his scythe or extended debates at Windsor Castle.

Garfield does the best he can with the material, but by the time Ploughman has a righteous and rageful awakening, it is far too late. And the failure of the film to nail the uneasy parallels to today’s political life feels like looking a gift horse in the mouth. There’s certainly a lot of points of identification for a modern audience with downtrodden people who don’t feel heard by the powers that be, but Greengrass barely lets the audience pause for breath, let alone trust them to join those dots.

A couple of weeks before release, the US distributor Focus Features briefly changed the film’s title to The Uprising: The Rise of Robin Hood, suggesting that it would show events “that helped inspire the legend of Robin Hood”, even though the Peasants’ Revolt took place nearly 200 years after the time of the folkloric outlaw and his merry men. Meanwhile, The Uprising makes no mention of Robin Hood: almost as if it was all a last-ditch attempt to drum up buzz for a movie that is about as fun as trench foot.

The Uprising is out in the US on 11 September, the UK on 9 October and Australia on 22 October

The Gate theatre’s creative daring gave a tiny stage international scope

The Guardian Wed, 09 Sep 2026 12:36:16 GMT

For five decades, this enterprising venue – which is now shutting up shop – broadened the horizons of British theatre

London’s Gate theatre, not to be confused with its Dublin namesake, is no more. A combination of factors, including rising costs, declining funding and its move in 2022 from its original home in Notting Hill Gate, means that it will cease trading next month. But it is worth celebrating its achievement over five decades. It has been an astonishing nursery of talent and has always stood for a defiant internationalism. “I sometimes think,” I once wrote, “that one learns more about world drama at the Gate than at any other London theatre.”

That was the dream of its founder, Lou Stein, who in 1979 took a tiny room over the Prince Albert pub and turned it into a 56-seat theatre that kicked off with Flann O’Brien’s At Swim-Two-Birds. You climbed the pub’s well-worn stairs and found yourself in a space that embraced the world. Not only that. In 1982 Stein launched an offshoot above another pub, the Latchmere in Battersea, where I still recall Susannah York as the Amazonian protagonist of Kleist’s Penthesilea.

Where Stein led others followed. His successor was Giles Croft, who ran the Gate from 1985 to 1989 and, taking a snapshot of his final year, I find the following list of shows: two Russian plays in Denis Fonvizin’s The Infant and Bulgakov’s Adam and Eve, a Marivaux double bill of The Colony and Island of Slaves, Heiner Müller’s The Task and a neglected English classic in Susannah Centlivre’s The Wonder. Nowhere else in the UK could you find a programme of such rich eclecticism.

Stephen Daldry took over in 1989 and I remember this young man in specs and scuffed sneakers standing at the top of the stairs welcoming people to the theatre as if they were guests in his home. Daldry not only introduced thematic programming – one of his seasons was called Women in World Theatre – he also showed that anything is possible in a small space. One of his discoveries was of a Bavarian dramatist, Marieluise Fleisser whose Pioneers in Ingoldstadt from the 1920s involved, in Ian MacNeil’s breathtaking design, a cast of 30 crossing a bridge. I recall Daldry telling me that such ventures were only possible because the Gate was unsubsidised: plug into public funding and it would not only be artistically accountable but would also have to pay Equity rates.

Daldry was clearly a brilliant director. He also encouraged others. It was at the Gate that I first became aware of Katie Mitchell through her productions of Euripides’ Women of Troy and Gorky’s Vassa Zheleznova in which Paola Dionisotti in the title role memorably demonstrated the private cost of capitalist success. Daldry stimulated another young director and his eventual successor, Laurence Boswell, to pursue his obsession with Spanish drama. It was thanks to Boswell that we got to know such classics as Tirso de Molina’s Don Gil of the Green Breeches, Lope de Vega’s The Gentleman from Olmedo and The Great Pretenders in which Louis Hilyer was an actor-manager who so identified with a Christian martyr he was playing that he ended up being spectacularly crucified.

If I dwell on those early years it was because the Gate, particularly during the mean and insular Thatcherite 80s, was proving that there was a world elsewhere and that it was possible to create infinite riches in a little room. But all the directors who followed put their own individual stamp on the Gate. During David Farr’s tenure we saw Sarah Kane’s incest-dominated Phaedra’s Love. Mick Gordon’s reign gave us Peter Hall’s staging in 2000 of Giuseppe Manfridi’s Cuckoos, which showed two lovers permanently stuck in an act of anal intercourse: for all its sensational surface a genuine domestic tragedy.

A succession of female directors went on to reconfigure the space while extending the repertory. Erica Whyman staged a season of adapted Greek myths. Thea Sharrock gave us a shattering production of O’Neill’s The Emperor Jones, later seen at the Olivier, with Paterson Joseph as the fugitive hero. The joint tenure of Carrie Cracknell and Natalie Abrahami saw Lucy Kirkwood’s post-Ibsenite Hedda and Christopher Haydon and Ellen McDougall each valiantly kept the show on the road while reinforcing the Gate’s capacity to take one by surprise. But when it left its Notting Hill Gate premises and moved to Camden Town it inevitably sacrificed some of its identity. Other London theatres, such as the Almeida, the Finborough and the Arcola, were increasingly venturing into the territory it had once owned. The public funding which Daldry had once eschewed also proved unreliable. But, while dwelling on the Gate’s demise, we should glory in its success in enhancing so many careers and in showing that the one sure way for a small theatre to make its mark is by taking gigantic risks.

Call My Agent! The Movie review – the gang get back together and c’est formidable

The Guardian Wed, 09 Sep 2026 12:00:47 GMT

The screwball French comedy is back as a film that actually works, thanks to putting Andréa and Noémie at the heart of chaotic events and bringing all the old faces back

At last: a beloved-TV-show-to-film-spinoff that doesn’t suck! The original French series is a screwball-speed office comedy about a boutique Parisian talent agency, and was a ratings and critical success in its homeland when it started back in 2015. Its acquisition by Netflix grew the audience internationally and spawned a stable full of remakes across Europe and Asia. In the meantime, several members of the original French cast have become proper stars in their own right, especially Camille Cottin and Laure Calamy, and this sequel, set five years on, is smart to put these two at the heart of the latest instalment. And of course, there are the obligatory turns from properly famous actors playing themselves, including Laetitia Casta, Vincent Macaigne, Laurent Lafitte and some guy named George Clooney, best known these days for appearances on vaporettos in the Venice lagoon.

Like many great sitcoms, this one always understood that failure, rather than success, keeps the wider narrative arc more interesting and relatable. So the last episode of the series left the gang at talent agency ASK (which stood for Agence Samuel Kerr, after the founder, who died in the first episode), dispersed to new gigs and careers; the band, in effect, broke up. Five years on, the stars have aligned to bring them all back together to work on Andréa (Cottin) and Noémie’s (Calamy) new film project, so the title Call My Agent! The Movie works on more than one level.

So now, silver fox smoothie Mathias (Thibault de Montalembert) is running a small agency with his daughter Camille (Fanny Sidney) while Mathias and his secretary-lover Noémie are finally officially together. Noémie, always a natural organiser, has become a producer with her own hit TV show that looks suspiciously just like Call My Agent! Thanks to complicated (and mostly backfiring) machinations on Mathias’s part, Noémie ends up producing their former colleague Andréa’s first feature as a writer-director.

Enter Casta and Macaigne as the leads of the film within the film, the latter represented by ASK alumnus Gabriel (Grégory Montel), who went off to be the token nice guy for a hateful all-business rival agency. Andréa has in the interim split up with her girlfriend and co-parent Colette (Ophélia Kolb), although that means we get a custody battle to add a bit of drama. Thankfully, everyone’s favourite comic reliefs, old salt Arlette (Liliane Rovère) and assistant turned actor Hervé (Nicolas Maury) are still in the ensemble – even if Arlette is somewhat underused until the last act.

Writers Fanny Herrero, Lison Daniel and Violaine Bellet, along with director Émilie Noblet, skilfully open the tap and let the stream of industry-insider jokes flow at an even pace but make sure that the final product never feels smug, sentimental or self-congratulatory. The energy flags a tad in the midsection, but by the time Andréa’s film starts shooting and a cascade of bad luck descends on the set to wreak havoc, the comedy hits its stride again. Formidable.

Call My Agent! The Movie is on Netflix from 10 September.

‘Courage and contradictions’: what Gloria Steinem meant to feminist writers from around the world

The Guardian Wed, 09 Sep 2026 11:39:02 GMT

Our global panel of writers reflect on the great legacy of the American feminist and civil rights activist, who died last week aged 92

Rebecca Solnit

Guardian US columnist and author

As far as I can tell, the US women’s movement was mostly clustered in coastal cities and university towns until Ms magazine, which Gloria Steinem cofounded and for many years co-managed, made it national. My mother in suburban California was an early subscriber and I was a tween who voraciously devoured every issue. I think it played a role in stiffening her resolve and her sense of her own rights, which led to her leaving my violent father.

Some of the hot takes I’m seeing now on Steinem, and the women’s movement she was at the heart of, act as reminders that a lot of people have no idea of what women’s lives were like before second-wave feminism. Of how women were routinely described as weaker, less intelligent, less rational and less objective than men, and therefore less believable, less qualified to work, testify, participate. No understanding of how utterly disempowered and excluded women were in both law and society, how women were rendered radically unequal economically in so many ways, including exclusion from professions and education and without rights to equal pay, to be free from workplace sexual harassment and discrimination. No memory of how marriage was a relationship of radical inequality in which a woman surrendered many rights and her identity to her husband, not even reserving the right to say no to sex until pressure from feminists made marital rape a crime in a growing number of American states in the 1970s and 1980s.

We now face a huge backlash, maybe even huger than the backlash we’ve always faced, but I believe feminism is just getting going in reversing not centuries but millennia of patriarchy, and I’m grateful for the role Gloria Steinem played in giving those decades of the 1970s to 1990s the transformative momentum that has made my life so much better, in so many ways, than my mother’s, let alone my grandmother’s.

Rokhaya Diallo

French journalist, writer, film-maker, activist and Guardian Europe columnist

Gloria Steinem understood early on that the feminist struggle would be fought through the media as well as campaigning, and inspired generations of journalists, myself included. As co-founder of Ms magazine, the first in the US run entirely by women, she strengthened the connection between journalism and activism.

Steinem’s feminism was more attentive to race than that of many of her white contemporaries in the “second wave”. Her first explicitly feminist essay, After Black Power, Women’s Liberation, displays a keen understanding of the need to connect feminist struggles with other movements for justice. She wrote about poor women and mothers, and imagined an alliance between radical feminists, middle-class women and “poor women of all colors”, although some of the dated terminology may now appear offensive. Her relationships with prominent women of colour – including Dorothy Pitman Hughes, Shirley Chisholm and Wilma Mankiller – informed every aspect of her work. As she acknowledged: “Personally, I learned feminism disproportionately from Black women.” In 1971, she served as treasurer of the fund for the legal defence of Angela Davis, the Black feminist philosopher unjustly prosecuted for murder who faced the death penalty.

Steinem leveraged her privilege as an educated white woman with access to elite media circles, but could not escape the dynamics of public life that made hers “the face of feminism” within a diverse and collective movement: the names of the women of colour who stood alongside her have not left the same imprint on public memory.

While I admired Steinem immensely, I regretted that her feminism remained so closely aligned with the Democratic party. This led her to defend Bill Clinton in 1998 and minimise Monica Lewinsky’s allegations, before acknowledging this failing two decades later. Her support for Hillary Clinton also exposed the limits of a feminism centred on representation.

But at a time of rising femonationalism (the use of women’s rights to advance nationalist and racist agendas), Steinem’s legacy reminds us of the urgent need for a feminism rooted in international solidarity and committed to fighting every form of oppression.

Mona Eltahawy

Egyptian-American journalist and author of the FEMINIST GIANT newsletter

A couple of days after Egyptian riot police assaulted me during a protest near Tahrir Square in November 2011, Gloria Steinem emailed me with news of what she called my “girl gang”: feminists and activists from around the world who had been writing to each other to find the best ways to support me. “No matter where you are, please tell me if there is anything at all I can do to make your life easier – or our outrage more effective, with friendship and empathy from your Girl Gang!” she signed off.

I had met Gloria just once, a month before, when the Hammer museum in Los Angeles hosted us for a feminist conversation in front of a live audience. She was a gracious interlocutor who treated me like a peer. We met several times since that conversation, each a reminder of the power of the feminist girl gang.

I was among a girl gang of 25 that she invited to send her questions for an Interview magazine column. My question was about us both being childfree by choice. “I would put the emphasis on ‘free’. It has increased my freedom,” she replied.

I am a feminist who will tell you to fuck off to your face. Kindness and empathy did not make it to my second book, The Seven Necessary Sins for Women and Girls. Gloria blurbed it thus: “Mona Eltahawy’s Necessary Sins is shocking, brave, gloriously unfeminine, and right on time … Reading it will free you, and acting on it will free us all.”

My “sins” – anger, profanity, violence etc – are necessary in our fight against patriarchy. Gloria’s kindness and empathy were like steroids that strengthened us for that fight: batons she passed across feminist generations and borders – and especially vital when that fight against patriarchy leaves us bruised, with broken limbs, and broke. She lent me $1,000 during a particularly tight financial time and I was mortified at how long it took me to repay her. She was unfazed.

Farewell, Gloria. To quote your 2011 email: “you should see the … loving outpouring from your girl gang from around the world!”

V (formerly Eve Ensler)

American playwright and activist

I will always be grateful to Gloria for her early support of my play The Vagina Monologues. After she came to see me perform in a little theatre way downtown, she agreed to write the foreword to the book. She showed up decking her red boa at every event we held early on to birth the V-Day movement to end violence against women, gender-expansive people and girls – now 30 years old – into the world. The Vagina Monologues was very outside the mainstream at the time and her support of it helped other people be brave.

She did that same thing for so many women, catalysing their dreams, their visions, their advocacy, their emerging non-profits by lending her support, her strategy, her kindness.

It’s not lost on me that Gloria left this world in the midst of one of the greatest periods of attacks on women’s rights – the destruction of maternal health care; women being forced out of the labour market in the hundreds of thousands, especially Black women; the siege on reproductive rights; rape academies emerging online; the Epstein files still not being prosecuted; and having a convicted felon as president who has been found liable in a civil court for sexual abuse. But if Gloria had anything, she had stamina and infinite hope, and she would want us to remember that the backlash is an indication of our victories and our power.

Now we need to go beyond where we’ve been, to new imaginings in order to fight off the racist, fascist, capitalist patriarchy that is actively working to kill our world.

Julia Gillard

Former Australian prime minister and former leader of the Australian Labor party. She was the first woman to hold either position

I am deeply saddened by the passing of feminist icon Gloria Steinem. Gloria was at the vanguard of the women’s rights movement as a political activist, journalist and editor, writer and thinker for more than 60 years. It is impossible to write the history of the women’s movement without her name being at the centre of the narrative. Indeed, her name is synonymous with feminism.

I felt incredibly fortunate to interview Gloria in 2022 for A Podcast of One’s Own. Then 88, Gloria was as passionate as ever about achieving equality and advocating for others. I greatly admired her steadfast commitment to the cause, even when progress was not linear, and backwards steps were taken – especially for reproductive freedom in the United States.

Gloria’s dedication to equality and empowerment for women everywhere, and from all walks of life, will continue to endure around the world. Her legacy is now ours to take forward. My heartfelt condolences go out to Gloria’s family and friends.

Jennifer Robinson

Australian barrister working at at Doughty Street Chambers, and co-author of How Many More Women?

When I heard the news Gloria Steinem had died, everything stopped.

I had just walked out of the Sydney opening of our documentary, Silenced, which is about the legal backlash against #MeToo and how the law silences women from speaking out about abuse. Women were walking out of the cinema crying and angry about how far we still have to go – and activated about what we need to do to change it.

And then we were hit with the news that we had lost Steinem. The news spread by hushed whispers through in the crowd in front of me. The grief was palpable.

Steinem, the silence-breaker. The truth-teller who had inspired millions of women around the world to find our voices and use them. The woman who inspired my grandmother, my mother – and me. My grandmother is a survivor of domestic violence and later worked in the women’s refuge movement to make it easier for the women and children who came after her. She is in our film because her work inspired mine. I grew up hearing my grandmother quote Steinem and, whenever I speak – including the other night in Sydney – her words and her ideas can be found.

It hit me hard. I had to take a moment. I wanted to cry. But then I looked around at the sea of women in front of me – victim-survivors, frontline services workers, lawyers from women’s legal services, and engaged and concerned community members, inspired to help create the change we need for women.

It was beautiful. And it made me think of one of my favourite Steinem quotes: “People are always asking me, ‘Who will you pass the torch to?’ The question makes me angry. There is no one torch – there are many torches – and I’m using my torch to light other torches.”

In her lifetime, she lit so many torches – all over the world – including in me and among the women gathered with me in Sydney the other night. What an incredible legacy.

As she said, “The future depends entirely on what each of us does every day; a movement of people is only people moving.” The best way to celebrate and honour her legacy is to continue it – and keep moving.

Elif Shafak

British-Turkish novelist and political scientist

In my mid-20s I left Istanbul to become a fellow in women’s studies at Mount Holyoke College in Massachusetts. I arrived without knowing a single soul, entranced by the splendour of autumnal colours in Boston. The libraries there hold one of the best archives in the US on the history of feminist theory and practice, and, as winter descended, I burrowed myself into reading Audre Lorde, Maya Angelou, Doris Lessing, Toni Morrison … and that was when I properly discovered Gloria Steinem.

Steinem had an unconventional, nomadic upbringing, and until she was 11 she had not spent a full year at school. In the absence of stable education, it was books – including Louisa May Alcott’s Little Women – that helped and guided her. “I was rescued by librarians,” she would explain later.

I was struck by the courage she had shown in exposing the reality of the shiny world of Playboy bunny clubs, and the magazine she co-founded, Ms, never shied from covering difficult issues, such as sex trafficking and sexual harassment. But it was her books that stayed with me: Moving Beyond Words, Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellions, Marilyn: Norma Jean …

Steinem believed that any meaningful change had to grow like a tree. From the bottom up. She not only founded women’s organisations and became a leading voice in second-wave feminism, she also saw the women’s movement as her chosen family. She said she had learned feminism from Black women. For her, race and gender were inextricably connected: “It is not possible to be a feminist without being anti-racist.” She was equally cognisant of class barriers. She passionately wanted to connect local, national and global feminisms.

When people asked her how she managed to remain optimistic, she said it was because she did not stay in one place. Just like in her childhood, she kept travelling. “Perhaps the most revolutionary act for a women will be a self-willed journey – and to be welcomed when she comes home.”

She was not perfect and not always right, and we also need to be able to talk about that – in a calm and nuanced way. Her contribution to generations of civil rights and women’s rights has been immense and genuine. Gloria Steinem would have made a fascinating character in a novel – with her resilience, her courage, her determination, her trailblazing and her contradictions.

Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett

British Guardian columnist

I first encountered Gloria Steinem in much the same way as I met her feminist contemporaries – on my mother’s bookshelves, which I ransacked. Although as a teenage girl in the late 1990s I had very much swallowed the post-feminist narrative (much to my mother’s disappointment) that the women’s movement had accomplished all it needed to, I still read every book for adult women that I could get my hands on. I credit Steinem’s undercover Playboy Bunny piece – which was extracted in one of the books – with the fact that I started to question the raunch culture that was all around me (and never bought a Playboy T-shirt). That is the power of good journalism – it echoes through the decades.

I found Steinem again at university, in the aftermath of a violent attack that galvanised me, as it can so many women, and have been a great admirer ever since. When I was in my 20s, setting up my own feminist magazine – the Vagenda – her work was a big influence. Her vocal and inclusive activism, her willingness to reflect on her missteps, her sense of humour and her refusal to give up the fight even when times were very dark indeed have all been an inspiration.

Her book dedication to the British doctor who granted her an abortion at the age of 22 despite it not then being legal – in which she writes “I’ve done the best that I could with my life”, as she had promised him he would – struck a chord with so many for a reason: it’s a profoundly moving testament to the freedom that access to abortion grants a woman, even more so in the aftermath of the repeal of Roe v Wade. I find it so very sad that Steinem leaves a world where reproductive rights remain under severe threat. She devoted her life to this and other crucial questions of women’s liberation. She would not give up the fight, and nor must we. Onwards, in her honour.

Inglourious baristas: why is Brad Pitt making coffee for 16 abusive dogs?

The Guardian Wed, 09 Sep 2026 10:30:04 GMT

In new film The Heart of the Beast, the A-lister’s bond with his loyal mutt proves crucial. In Spike Jonze’s new advert, Pitt is rather more subservient

Brad Pitt has a new movie out this month, The Heart of the Beast, about an emotionally damaged man who forms a life-saving bond with a dog. If that sounds familiar, maybe it is because you have seen The Call of the Wild. Or maybe it is because you have seen A Dog’s Way Home. Or maybe it is because you have seen Dog. Or, look, you get the idea.

But perhaps Brad Pitt knows that getting people to see something as unimaginative as The Heart of the Beast is an uphill struggle, because that would explain why he has just made an advert that looks and feels much more like the Brad Pitt dog movie that deserves to be made. In short, it is an advert where Brad Pitt gets loudly disparaged by a number of dogs for an extended period of time.

As reported by Variety, the commercial is for the De’Longhi Magnifica Duo, an all-singing, all-dancing coffee machine that retails in the UK for about £700. But really the product is beside the point. The main point is that the advert, running to almost two minutes, sees Brad Pitt stumble around cluelessly while a small army of real dogs – all of whom have names, some of whom are dressed in human clothes – shout insults at him.

As he wanders into his living room, some of the dogs (in subtitle) tell him that he woke up too late. They tell him to make a hot coffee and, even though he has started to make a cold one, he drops his head and sullenly obliges. Then another dog says that he can’t have any coffee at all until his attitude improves. “OK,” he mumbles in return, like a put-upon sitcom dad. The dogs berate him for his slovenliness and his stupidity and, when he finally snaps and tells them to go and fetch a stick, they make him fetch a stick for them instead.

It’s a weird advert. It is slightly reminiscent of that bizarre Chinese commercial for Chinese vitamins from a few years back, when Tom Hiddleston cooks you breakfast before looking straight into your eyes and promising that he’s going to have sex with you. The difference is that, while you could tell that Hiddleston desperately hoped that nobody would see his ad, Pitt’s has been made for an American market. He wants you to see this.

Of course, it helps that the weirdness is deliberate. The commercial was directed by Spike Jonze, the visionary director of no films at all for the last 13 years. The world has been crying out for a new film by Jonze, and if the closest we’re going to get is a film where Brad Pitt gets insulted by a dog named Kyle, then that will have to do.

In fact, the more you consider it, the better a move this advert seems for Pitt. Compared with the derivative grit-jawed Americana of The Heart of the Beast, it demonstrates that he’s much better when he’s allowed to be funny. And if it underlines a connection between Pitt and dogs along the way, creating an implied synergy with his movie, then that’s OK too.

It’s also a big step up from Pitt’s previous De’Longhi commercials, the majority of which just required him to stand still and smoulder for a while. Those commercials could have starred anyone. You could have put a carrot on human growth hormones and it would have adequately done the job. At least this one has a bit of personality.

Only the De’Longhi sales team will know if this has been a successful gambit or not, but speaking personally I think it works perfectly. With any luck it will bring Spike Jonze out of retirement, and Brad Pitt Gets Shit-Talked by Some Dogs will be a motion picture by next Christmas.

Want to start lazymaxxing? Here are some low-effort ways to improve your life

The Guardian Wed, 09 Sep 2026 10:00:06 GMT

CEOs may like to get up at the crack of dawn and go for a run, but I prefer optimising my life with lie-ins, trashy films, swearing and coffee

This evening I’m going to tuck my five-year-old into bed and read her a chapter from one of her princess books, followed by a summary of research recently presented at the annual congress of the European Society of Cardiology. Once upon a time, I’ll tell her, there was a scientist called Dr Nawon Lee who authored a study that found having a weekend lie-in may be very good for you and can protect against high blood pressure. Our accomplished protagonist Dr Lee said: “People should not feel lazy or guilty for sleeping a little longer on the weekend.” And the moral of this story, dear child, is that you should try not to wake your mothers up at 6am every day.

Unfortunately, I’m not sure that all the peer-reviewed science in the world will convince my early riser to have a weekend lie-in. Still, as a big fan of sleep and someone who has never once felt guilty for hitting the snooze button, I have to say I feel vindicated by this new study. CEOs can get up at 4am and run 10 miles before eating five foraged mushrooms if they want to, but I’m going to protect my heart health by sleeping in, any opportunity I can get, thank you very much.

The rich world is currently in thrall to tech-enabled self-optimisation. Or as some people (people you do not want to end up seated next to at a dinner party) call it: humanmaxxing. We’re told we should track our biomarkers and optimise every second of our days, often in complicated and joyless ways. If that works for you, great. But, personally, I’m a big fan of lazymaxxing and finding low-effort ways to improve my life. Weekend lie-ins are obviously one, drinking coffee is another. A 2025 study found that morning coffee drinkers were 16% less likely to die early of any cause. Swearing is also surprisingly good for you: uttering a profanity can decrease physical pain and increase focus. And while I can’t go so far as to say that bingeing Love is Blind has health-giving properties, I did unearth research concluding that enjoying trashy films is a sign you’re a well-educated cultural omnivore. I still haven’t found a study proving that lying on the couch, eating crisps, reading thrillers and ignoring your obligations is good for you, but I live in hope.

NFL 2026 season predictions: which teams can bring down the Rams juggernaut?

The Guardian Wed, 09 Sep 2026 08:00:04 GMT

The new season kicks off on Wednesday night. Our writers have their say on the MVP, rookies to watch and the disasters waiting to happen

Quarterbacks living under center. The NFL has developed into a shotgun league, where most quarterbacks take the majority of their snaps three to seven yards away from the center. But the increase in efficiency when it comes to snaps taken right behind the center should have coaches directing their quarterbacks to do more of it. Matthew Stafford, Caleb Williams, and Sam Darnold led the way in 2025, and others will follow. DF

Superteams. The Rams have pushed their chips to the middle of the table by loading up on high-end veterans and deferring much of the cost to future years. Myles Garrett and the unretired Aaron Donald join Stafford, Puka Nacua and a secondary reinforced by Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson. Superteams are never a sure thing in the NFL, but the Rams’ terrifyingly stacked roster looks awfully close. BAG

Super Bowl sequel hype, the year the scriptwriters lay a path for a Rams-Bengals rematch in Los Angeles. Both teams have gone to considerable lengths to shore up the defensive side of the ball, with the Rams swinging a mega trade for Garrett on the heels of the Bengals’ draft-week swap for Pro Bowl tackle Dexter Lawrence. AL

Finally saying goodbye to Aaron Rodgers. Let’s forget all the weirdness around the latter years of his career and remember Rodgers as simply one of the best to ever do it. Maybe with Mike McCarthy calling plays again, he can keep Pittsburgh in contention for a wildcard. Even if he fails, you can guarantee seeing some of the old magic in his final season in the NFL. GS

This is the second straight season I’ve pushed the Vikings here, and for the same reasons – the NFC North is the league’s most competitive division, and there is no outstanding candidate at quarterback. Brian Flores’s defense will be marvelous as it always is, and were it not for his ongoing lawsuit against the league, he’d probably be a head coach right now. A three-man quarterback competition is not the best way to maximize one’s competitive window, though. DF

Dak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb are back for an offense that can put up points with almost anybody. But the NFC is deep and unforgiving and the Cowboys’ front seven looks alarmingly short of difference-makers beyond star defensive tackle Quinnen Williams and Rashan Gary. Nine wins, constant frustration and a third straight January on the couch sounds about right. BAG

The Vikings’ defense always gives them a chance, and their offensive skill players are elite. It just comes down to what Murray can give them and, historically, that’s been a lot of inconsistency. AL

It will be a battle for Ben Johnson to keep the lightning in the bottle with a Bears defense that thrived on takeaways rather than fundamentals last season. They haven’t made many significant moves – outside first-round safety Dillon Thieneman – to tune things up, then the impressive offense could be let down with a near miss in the wildcard race. GS

It’s easy to forget that in the 2021 season, the Bengals lost the Super Bowl by three points, and in 2022, they lost the AFC Championship game by the same margin. Those close calls were followed by matching 9-8 seasons in 2023 and 2024, and last season’s 6-11 faceplant. But if Joe Burrow can stay healthy, these Bengals have a ton of talent on both sides of the ball (led by new defensive line monster Lawrence). DF

Justin Herbert is class and Mike McDaniel’s arrival as offensive coordinator will add some imagination and flair to the offense. But winning 11 games still leaves you overshadowed when Denver’s complete roster and Patrick Mahomes’ Kansas City headline your division. The Chargers are quiet contenders hiding in plain sight. BAG

Last I checked, the Chiefs not only return Patrick Mahomes – the QB standard before the ACL injury (hardly the career killers they used to be) – but also Eric Bieniemy, the offensive coordinator who held players accountable and infused the team’s gameplay with so much confidence and whimsy. AL

Baker Mayfield was quietly brilliant last season and the Buccaneers have a strong roster across the board that finished 8-9 after a 6-2 start because of a number of key players missing time through injury. A bit of luck with the injury bug and the Bucs could spring a surprise. GS

The Browns’ quarterback situation. What else could it be? At this point, the Browns may as well bring Manziel back to add even more of a tragic comic cast to the whole thing. Head coach Todd Monken naming Deshaun Watson the Week 1 starter after Watson played horribly and alienated the fanbase in the preseason – never mind the horrid off-field history for which Watson has never taken an ounce of accountability – is merely the first level of Dante’s Inferno. DF

Cleveland naming Watson their Week 1 starter. A $230m albatross coming off multiple achilles tears would have been a risky first choice even if he’d been playing well before getting hurt. The Browns’ decision to roster three other quarterbacks, including Dillon Gabriel on injured reserve, feels prescient here. BAG

Anthony Richardson survived trade rumors and played well enough in camp to win the Colts’ backup QB job. But I say the detente only holds up as long as Daniel Jones’s health, which has never been the greatest, and Richardson’s uneven play in relief makes him a lame duck QB all over again – and his controversial behavior gives the organization cover for the bad fit once more. AL

The Browns missing Garrett’s tremendous pass rush and leadership is a recipe for a very tricky season if they make a slow start. And with Watson starting at quarterback they most likely will. GS

Drake Maye, QB, New England Patriots. While I don’t have the Patriots winning the AFC East this season, I think that with the additions of receivers AJ Brown and Romeo Doubs, and coming off a full season in Josh McDaniels’ offense, Maye has everything he needs to take the next step to become an unquestioned Top 10 quarterback. He was exactly that until the Patriots faced a murderers’ row of defenses in the playoffs and his protection fell apart, but the growth he showed in everything from reading the field to taking disguised coverages apart presaged that next level. DF

Lamar Jackson, QB, Baltimore Ravens. The Ravens enter a new era under first-year coach Jesse Minter, but their fortunes still revolve around the NFL’s most disruptive player. The 29-year-old Jackson can unhinge defenses with his arm, legs or simply the threat of either. If Baltimore can get to 12 or 13 wins, he becomes the best bet to enter the exclusive club of three-time MVPs. BAG

Joe Burrow, QB, Cincinnati Bengals. Now that he has a defense behind him again, Joe Cool can get back to lighting up the scoreboard and his cigar after the dubs. AL

Joe Burrow, QB, Cincinnati Bengals. The quarterback finished last year showing some of his best work, so this could be Burrow’s time with incredible weapons Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins at his disposal. GS

Caleb Downs, DB, Dallas Cowboys. The Cowboys’ 2025 defense was one of the worst in recent memory, which is why they replaced Matt Eberflus with Christian Parker as defensive coordinator. Parker’s background with the Philadelphia Eagles and defensive wizard Vic Fangio should pay immediate dividends, and Downs, the Ohio State alum selected with the 11th overall pick, should thrive in Parker’s concepts. DF

Jadarian Price, RB, Seattle Seahawks. With Kenneth Walker III gone and Zach Charbonnet starting the season on the Physically Unable to Perform list, the Seahawks will plug-and-play their first-round draft pick from Notre Dame into a backfield fresh off a Super Bowl title. BAG

Jeremiyah Love, RB, Arizona Cardinals. The Notre Dame prospect shouldn’t lack for opportunities to get the ball off tackle, in space or however else coach Mike LaFleur seeks to make use of the Saquon Barkley clone he simply couldn’t pass up in this year’s draft. AL

Carnell Tate, WR, Tennessee Titans. The No 4 pick has the total package of speed, route running and size. Tate caught the eye in training camp working with second-year quarterback Cam Ward. He will continue to do so throughout 2026. GS

I’m picking the Bills for one reason, and it’s not Josh Allen – it’s Jim Leonhard. Buffalo’s new defensive coordinator is one of the finest minds in football, and he’ll have that defense asserting itself in ways it never did under Sean McDermott. New England will still be up there after 2025’s Cinderella season, but a tougher schedule and possible regression when it comes to their unusual injury luck should have them taking a step back. DF

New England won it last year and added star wideout Brown, but a regression from 14 wins is almost inevitable even if the Super Bowl loser’s curse has mostly been debunked. The Bills have Allen, DJ Moore and enough defensive talent for first-year coach Joe Brady to take back a division the Bills owned for five straight years before last season. BAG

Not because the Bills are necessarily better than the team that beat them to the top last year. But because New England’s schedule is so much tougher this year, and one loss makes all the difference in this chilly rivalry. AL

A straight shootout between New England and Buffalo. With fresh ideas from Brady, the Bills could have an important edge but there’s not much wriggle room in their opening five games against the Texans, Lions, Chargers, Patriots and Rams. Escaping with a winning record from that run would provide a solid platform to regain dominance. GS

Trading for Lawrence was the splashy story of the Bengals’ offseason, but there’s a lot more to like here – especially if Burrow can stay healthy. If he can, I like the Bengals to outpace the Ravens and Steelers based on star power with receivers Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, and a defense that has a lot of ascending players. DF

Minter has been dealt an enviable hand with Jackson, Derrick Henry and a roster built to win now. Cincinnati should push them, but the Ravens’ combination of quarterback play, running game and defensive stability remains the division’s safest bet. BAG

The Bengals. Here’s a sentence no one’s ever written until now: Mike Brown, the NFL’s resident cheapskate, is all in. AL

If Burrow just has a full season working behind an improved offensive line, then the Bengals have a great shot at unseating the Ravens. Their schedule is soft enough that they should be aiming for well over 10 wins. GS

I’m taking the Texans over the Jaguars because of a defense that needs no schematic tricks to upend enemy offenses – they’re good enough to just line up and go right at you. All the Texans need from quarterback CJ Stroud is a level of play a bit above league-average. DF

The Texans defense is one of the NFL’s best with Will Anderson Jr, Derek Stingley Jr and Kamari Lassiter leading the way. Whether Stroud and the offense can hold up their end of the bargain remains the rub, but it should be enough in this middling division. BAG

The Jaguars repeatedly found ways to win tight games in 2025, giving a young team meaningful late-game experience – and a plausible foundation to turn last year’s surge into a deep postseason run. AL

The defense returns almost unchanged after a brilliant 2025 with some good additions in safety Reed Blankenship and rookie run-stopper Kayden McDonald. The Texans have quality and consistency a level above the messy Jaguars and Colts. GS

I really like what new Chargers offensive coordinator McDaniel will do for Herbert, and I expect the Chiefs to rebound to a point from last season’s disaster. But the 2025 Broncos got all the way to the AFC Championship game, and they may have progressed further had quarterback Bo Nix not suffered a broken ankle in the divisional round. Now, Nix has a new best buddy to help him – former Miami Dolphins receiver Jaylen Waddle, who gives that offense a level of vertical juice it hasn’t had before. DF

They’d probably be defending NFL champions if not for Nix’s untimely injury in the playoffs. The Broncos defense remains elite, the offensive line is right there with it and the addition of Waddle gives them another weapon on offense alongside Courtland Sutton. Nix’s mission with the AFC’s deepest roster boils down to three words: do no harm. BAG

The Chargers made many of the right moves this offseason: keeping most of their receiving corps intact, adding David Njoku and big-play tailback Keaton Mitchell, and rebuilding the interior offensive line. Losing new center Tyler Biadasz to injury is a major blow, but if the line holds together well enough, Herbert and a deep, balanced roster give the Bolts a real chance to edge Kansas City and Denver. AL

The Chiefs and Chargers should be well in the mix but the Broncos still have the edge after last year’s dominance before Nix went down in the playoffs. GS

The Cowboys bag the crown based on an offense that’s already fully loaded, and a defense that should be worlds better than in 2025. They are the Inverse Houston Texans in that all that defense has to do is play at a pretty good level to blow a lot of opponents away. DF

Brown is gone and Jalen Hurts will be working with his seventh different play-caller in as many NFL seasons, but the Eagles’ institutional strength has been the envy of the NFC East for decades now. A potentially top-five defense and a rejuvenated ground game featuring Saquon Barkley will provide enough margin for error to outlast a division filled with flawed rivals. BAG

With Brown and coordinator Kevin Patullo gone, the Eagles offense should fly again behind Barkley and Hurts – in make or break year mode not that long after leading the team to Super Bowl glory. AL

The Cowboys are hardly a sleeping giant, but if the defense is as reborn as defensive tackle Williams claims it is then maybe Dallas can finally balance the books with their dynamic offense and reclaim the division. GS

Close your eyes and throw a dart at the NFL’s toughest division, and you have a 25% chance of being right. The Lions, Packers, and Vikings all have reason for hope, but if Bears head coach Ben Johnson can refine quarterback Caleb Williams, and Dennis Allen’s defense can improve over last season’s boom-or-bust results – they led the NFL in turnover differential, but ranked 23rd in points allowed – it’s Chicago’s time to shine. DF

Chicago may be the trendy pick and Green Bay dangerous floaters, but the Lions still have enough offensive firepower and strength along the line of scrimmage to hold them off in the NFL’s deepest division. BAG

The Lions were burned by injuries last year and still stayed in the playoff hunt almost to the end. They are positioned for a rebound, with more of their core available and one of the league’s easiest schedules – a chance to bank early wins while key pieces work their way back from early-season absences. AL

The Packers remain without Micah Parsons until at least Week 5 but a look at their first four opponents – the Vikings, Jets, Falcons and Buccaneers – points to a hot start. GS

Mayfield was outstanding in the first half of the 2025 season before his own injuries, and the injuries of those around him, took their toll. The Buccaneers started the season 6-2 before falling off to 8-9. With better luck things should look quite a bit better in 2026. DF

The Buccaneers have the most settled quarterback situation, enough skill-position talent and a defense that’s just good enough. Carolina are the likeliest threat while neither Atlanta nor rebuilding New Orleans have enough to mount a serious challenge. BAG

There’s little incentive to go against the Buccaneers, the gold standard in the league’s most volatile division. AL

Off the back of late-season success in 2025, the Saints will be feeling good about their chances. If second-year quarterback Tyler Shough maintains his upward trajectory they should be confident. GS

While there are reasons to question the ultimate validity of the Rams’ “all-in” approach that culminated with the return of Donald, there’s enough in the hypothetical to give Sean McVay’s team a slight edge over the Seahawks – if only because Seattle didn’t follow their Super Bowl win by radically stocking their defense as the Rams did. DF

There are legitimate durability questions around the aging Stafford and the returning Donald for the Rams. But it’s hard to imagine anyone challenging a roster tricked out with as much high-end talent as any NFL team in years. Anything short of a division title would qualify as a serious underachievement. BAG

The Rams. With apologies to the reigning Super Bowl champs, the moves GM Les Snead and Co made in the offseason to shore up their defense are eerily similar to the big swings they took in the 2021 season. And we all know how that turned out. AL

Donald and Garrett have five defensive player of the year awards between them and link up with former Super Bowl winners from the Chiefs in Watson and McDuffie. The Rams are stacked and then some. GS

Patriots, Jaguars, Chargers. DF

Patriots, Bengals, Chargers. BAG

Patriots, Ravens, Chiefs. AL

Chargers, Ravens, Jaguars. GS

Seahawks, Lions, Eagles. DF

Seahawks, Packers, Bears. BAG

Seahawks, 49ers, Cowboys. AL

Buccaneers, Lions, Seahawks. GS

Bills over Broncos. DF

Broncos over Bills. BAG

Bengals over Jaguars. AL

Broncos over Bengals. GS

Rams over Seahawks. DF

Rams over Eagles. BAG

Rams over Seahawks. AL

Rams over Cowboys. GS

Rams over Bills. The Rams’ “F Them Picks” philosophy served them well when they gave up a ton of draft capital for Stafford, Jalen Ramsey, and Von Miller, and they won the Super Bowl as a result. If the 2026 Rams find that their go-for-broke philosophy works once again with a radical reshuffling of their defense, it’s hard to bet against them, because the offense was already so on point. DF

Rams over Broncos. The Rams have spent the offseason putting together a star-studded roster unlike anything we’ve seen in years, adding Garrett, McDuffie and Watson before Donald decided he wasn’t finished after all. Denver’s elite defense is capable of making it ugly, but Sean McVay’s embarrassment of riches on both sides of the ball will ultimately prove too much. BAG

Bengals over Rams. Burrow avenges the biggest loss in his career, and it’s in no small part thanks to Brown and player personnel director Duke Tobin pulling the trigger one last time on a piece that helps neutralize the effects of the Garrett-Donald pocket collapse (an extra guard, a fullback – don’t hold me to specifics). The confusion over what to make of Zac Taylor as a Super Bowl-winning coach quickly gives way to the confusion over what to make of a championship parade festooned with tributes to the world’s weirdest chili. In other words, the renovations on ancient Paycor Stadium pay for themselves. AL

Broncos over Rams. Denver can argue they were a broken ankle away from the Super Bowl last season. Handily for the Broncos they come back with almost an identical roster this year. They kept starting running back JK Dobbins and brought in Waddle to help out Sutton. The Broncos already have the AFC’s best defense to go with a sublime offensive line and exciting weapons that can take down the Rams. GS

European democracies are running out of time to turn away from the abyss

The Guardian Wed, 09 Sep 2026 05:00:01 GMT

Far-right parties, Maga ideology and Kremlin money are conniving to suffocate liberal idealism for another generation

Not all that long ago, Europe was a beacon of liberal idealism. One memoir recalls it as an era “comfortably saturated with confidence in the unfailing and binding power of tolerance and conciliation”. The economic system seemed obviously preferable to barbarous alternatives. “People honestly believed that the divergencies and the boundaries between nations and sects would gradually melt away into a common humanity,” the author added.

Those words could describe the spirit of globalisation at the turn of the millennium. They were written in the 1930s by Stefan Zweig, reflecting on the optimism of late 19th-century Vienna from the perspective of a Jewish émigré whose world had been destroyed by murderous nationalism. Zweig took his own life in 1942. He never saw fascism defeated. He couldn’t have imagined a renaissance of liberalism in the second half of the 20th century so complete as to attain a pitch of complacency rivalling the one he remembered from his childhood.

Now momentum is with the nationalists again. Victory for the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in the region of Saxony-Anhalt over the weekend is not the biggest electoral prize won by a far-right party in Europe in recent years, but it is one of the most shocking because it is Germany. No country had more to learn from history if it wanted to immunise its democracy against extremism. None pursued a more systematic programme of inoculation. The word for it is Vergangenheitsbewältigung – hard to say and tricky to translate, meaning roughly coming to terms with a shameful past.

There is no excuse of ignorance about the AfD’s rise. It is a knowing repudiation of atonement. The party flirts with Nazi imagery and embraces racist definitions of nationhood, seeking to deport Germans whose credentials it sees as biologically improper. It is extreme enough to induce squeamishness in Marine Le Pen, leader of France’s far-right National Rally (RN). She has spent years carefully cultivating respectability and is leading the polls ahead of next year’s presidential election. She doesn’t want to jeopardise her mainstream credentials by association with the unambiguous extreme.

That is less of an impediment across the Atlantic. Elon Musk is an AfD fan, deploying his control of X to boost the party’s campaign messages. Last year, the US vice-president, JD Vance, met Alice Weidel, AfD co-leader, during a visit to Munich. There was no space in his diary for Olaf Scholz, then the German chancellor. Clearly, the AfD meets the criteria for endorsement set out in Donald Trump’s national security strategy, which pledges support for “patriotic resistance” movements committed to halting the “civilisational erasure” of Europe by immigration.

In Britain, Nigel Farage could once have assumed entitlement to that status as an early and enthusiastic cheerleader for Trump. But in the competition for Maga accolades, Reform UK has lost ground to parties and people even further to the right – Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain; ultra-nationalist agitator Tommy Robinson; pretty much anyone who can muster a mob of blackshirts or a passing troll who catches Musk’s eye posting racist conspiracy theories online.

It would be absurd if it wasn’t so effective. “We never fall into the same abyss twice,” writes Éric Vuillard, the French novelist. “But we fall in the same way, in a mixture of ridicule and dread.”

The reach and pungency of the US right, drenched in white supremacism, interferes with Farage’s old strategy of banking far-right support and feinting moderation to make gains in the mainstream. Chasing credibility with fanatical racists in an international digital arena makes it hard to reassure a domestic analogue audience that he should be allowed near Downing Street.

The tension shows in Farage’s attitude to the AfD. He spoke at a rally for it in 2017. Now he describes it as a “mixed bag” of a party, whose cultural stances are “utterly respectable and decent” but whose enthusiasm for dictators is “very difficult”.

Farage has called AfD support for Vladimir Putin “hard to understand”. It can’t be that far beyond comprehension for a man who, in 2014, described the Russian president as the world leader he most admired, albeit “as an operator, not a human being”.

If Farage needs further insight into what might motivate a Kremlin fellow traveller, he could reach out to Reform’s former leader in Wales, Nathan Gill, who is serving a prison sentence for accepting bribes to make pro-Russian speeches in the European parliament when he was a Brexit party MEP.

Proximity to the Moscow line is a fairly reliable measure of fanaticism and venality on the spectrum from far-right to even further-right politics in Europe and the US. The same applies on the left, where a credulous appetite for Russian propaganda endures decades after the demise of Soviet ideology.

Thankfully, there is not much of a market in British politics for openly pandering to Putin. That is one reason why Trump is also unpopular, although opinion polls suggest he is viewed more favourably by Reform supporters than the wider public. Farage has stopped boasting of his White House connections, perhaps because they have dried up, or maybe because sycophantic flapping around a foreign tyrant, even an American one, doesn’t project strength in a wannabe prime minister.

It is striking how little the Reform leader has to say about the rest of the world and Britain’s place in it. The topic was hardly mentioned at the party’s annual conference last week.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

There was a theatrical appearance by Jordan Bardella, the young Le Pen protege and likely prime minister if she wins the presidency. He signed a legally meaningless “deal” with Farage on stopping small-boat traffic across the Channel and was immediately criticised back home for selling out to the UK. The likelihood of a French far-right government taking in more migrants as a policy favour to the UK is close to zero. Having xenophobic nationalists setting the agenda in Paris and London wouldn’t make relations easier, no matter what ideological amity they now claim.

As the architect of Brexit, Farage is one of the most consequential politicians of his generation, but he can’t plausibly claim it as an achievement, even when addressing an auditorium of loyal fans. They know it has failed as well as everyone else.

Farage probably misses the simplicity of his old crusade against Brussels. He might envy nationalist counterparts on the continent, who get to rail against liberal Europeanism while enjoying the economic and strategic privileges afforded by EU membership. They don’t have to explain why it’s so cold on the outside. They play the Eurosceptic game, mobilising the same resentments, targeting the same scapegoats, but modifying the demands in recognition that Farage’s victory was pyrrhic. It doesn’t pay to actually leave. The ambition is to capture the European project, not destroy it, although it amounts to the same thing if the transformation happens through connivance with Maga ideology and Kremlin money.

This doesn’t have to be Europe’s destiny. Nationalists do not form a monolithic bloc. The essence of their creed militates against cross-border partnership. Their egos generate more rivalries than alliances. Their selfishness sabotages deals. Countervailing forces can be mustered. There is no law of history that says a height of liberal optimism must be followed by an equivalent fall into chaos. The “binding power of tolerance and conciliation” was not defeated in the 20th century and it won’t be suffocated in this one either. We see the abyss. We can pass without plunging to the bottom.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist
