Why Trump’s Midterm ‘Convention’ Isn’t a Real Convention

The New York Times September 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

No nominations or formal party business will be happening, as they would at a traditional presidential convention. But the made-for-TV speeches will look much the same.

By Reid J. Epstein

Reid J. Epstein has attended national party conventions going back to 2012. He has seen a lot of balloons drop.

One thing is missing from President Trump’s midterm gathering for Republicans this week: any semblance of official party business that forms the backbone of traditional quadrennial conventions.

Essentially, Mr. Trump has stripped out all the perfunctory, yet necessary, parts of a typical presidential convention and kept the made-for-TV elements.

Only once before in modern political history, in 1982, has a national party held a midterm-year gathering in advance of the midterm elections. That event, held by Democrats, went so poorly that the next party chairman called such events “places for mischief” and canceled plans to do it again in 1986.

In Dallas, there will not be a roll call of states awarding delegates to a presidential nominee. There won’t even be a presidential nominee. Or voting delegates. Forget about subcommittees to determine the party’s rules and credentials.

Republicans will not be debating their party platform, though they did not really do that at the last two presidential conventions, either. By now, the party’s platform is generally whatever Mr. Trump decides it is.

Instead, the two-day gathering in Dallas is set to be a pair of six-hour — though perhaps much longer — advertisements for Mr. Trump and his political acolytes. The speakers are a parade of Trump supporters, many of whom are either in his cabinet or on the ballot this November.

Party conventions in presidential years usually take place in the summer, are scheduled to avoid the Olympic Games and are meant to be held when there are few other compelling TV options. This event comes after Labor Day and will compete for national attention against the first two nights of the N. F. L. season.

The 1982 Democratic midterm conference, as it was called then, followed similar events in 1974 and 1978 that were held in December, after the midterm elections. They were essentially kickoff events for the coming presidential elections — though in 1978, Senator Edward M. Kennedy upstaged President Jimmy Carter with a speech that foreshadowed their contentious primary campaign.

Last year Ken Martin, the Democratic National Committee chairman, floated holding a midterm convention, but the idea was quietly dropped.

Some things in Dallas will look familiar. Vice President JD Vance, who is set to speak on Thursday night, will play the role of potential future presidential contender. His speech will be inspected for both his loyalty to Mr. Trump and indications of his possible ambitions for 2028.

And you can bet that Mr. Trump will preside over a balloon drop, or maybe two of them. They were known to be among his favorite parts of the 2016 and 2024 conventions — and a spectacle that had to be skipped in 2020 when Republicans moved their convention outdoors because of the coronavirus pandemic.

Reid J. Epstein is a Times reporter covering campaigns and elections from Washington.

Saudi Oil Exports Plunge as Spread of War Shuts Off Shipping Routes

The New York Times September 09, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

With few good options for safely shipping oil, Saudi Arabia’s exports have fallen to a 13-year low.

By Jenny Gross and Lisa Friedman

Jenny Gross has written about shipping in the Middle East since the start of the war in Iran. Lisa Friedman has been covering the fallout on energy. They reported from London.

Saudi Arabia has made several quick pivots to keep its oil flowing since the start of the U. S. war with Iran.

Within weeks of Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz — once Saudi Arabia’s primary export route for oil — the kingdom turned to Plan B: bypassing the strait by ramping up exports through pipelines to the Red Sea.

When the Iranian-backed Houthi militia in Yemen announced a blockade in the Red Sea, Saudi Arabia used a new detour, sending ships north to a pipeline near the Suez Canal. This Mediterranean route is costlier and adds weeks to the voyage to Asia, where most of the country’s customers are.

Now Saudi Arabia, long the world’s biggest oil exporter, is facing yet another test of its ability to deliver its oil. Edging toward a full-blown war with the Houthis, Saudi officials said the kingdom would retaliate after the Houthis injured 73 civilians and hit energy facilities in the southern part of the kingdom.

Whatever comfort shipping companies may have found using the Red Sea before the most recent escalation “has clearly soured,” said Peter Sand, a shipping analyst at Xeneta.

A steady supply of Saudi oil is critical to keeping global energy prices stable, and the kingdom’s exports are already squeezed. Its oil exports fell last month to 3.2 million barrels a day, the lowest level in at least 13 years, according to data from Kpler, a maritime information company. In the past week only two Saudi Arabian cargoes passed through the Bab al-Mandab Strait to the Red Sea, the group found.

Source: Kpler.

By The New York Times

The challenge comes as oil prices surged past $100 a barrel on Wednesday amid escalating attacks between the United States and Iran. Iran said it had launched missiles at a U. S. base in Jordan and fired on two Navy destroyers in retaliation for American attacks that the U. S. military said had destroyed five Iranian oil tankers. One sailor was killed and one reported missing on Wednesday after a drone hit a ship off the coast of the United Arab Emirates, according to Dimitris Maniatis, the founder of Marisks, a maritime risk agency.

The recent attacks by Houthi militants, on top of escalating tension in the Strait of Hormuz, are forcing further trade shifts, underscoring how the war in Iran has scrambled the normal routes for doing business.

“For commercial shipping, the immediate concern is therefore not simply the number of individual attacks, but the expansion of targeting criteria and geography,” Mr. Maniatis said.

Fighting in Yemen intensified last week as the Houthis tried to capture territory that could give them more control over shipping routes through the Red Sea, according to local security officials. Since July 20, when the group announced a blockade of Saudi shipping through the Red Sea, the Houthis have claimed responsibility for at least seven attacks on ships headed to or from Saudi ports, said Allison Minor, a former U. S. deputy special envoy for Yemen.

One attack on a Saudi tanker in late August occurred in the central part of the Red Sea, in an area that had been considered the safest alternative to using the Bab al-Mandab Strait. That attack demonstrated that the threat was not confined to the southern Red Sea waters around Yemen, Mr. Maniatis said.

Ships without links to Saudi Arabia are continuing to use the Bab al-Mandab Strait, but at a lower rate. Transits through the strait in August were the fewest since July 2025, at an average of 35 per day, according to Leth Agencies, a maritime data company. The Houthis have been clear that the Red Sea is open for ships without Saudi ties because the Houthis want to avoid U. S. retaliation, said Ms. Minor, a director at the Atlantic Council.

Still, the latest escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis is worrying for global trade, said Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow focused on the Middle East at the Royal United Services Institute, a defense research group in London.

“You don’t need the Bab al-Mandab to be physically closed for this to have a lasting economic impact,” Dr. Ozcelik said. The Houthi attacks that began in late 2023 had already caused many major shipping companies to avoid the Red Sea altogether, taking a much longer route from Asia to Europe around the Cape of Good Hope off South Africa.

Although the Houthis and Saudi Arabia have been locked in conflict in Yemen since 2014, the U. S.-Israeli war with Iran has introduced a dangerous new regional element. The Houthis have their own political agenda, but their attacks on Saudi Arabia also fit the broader Iranian strategy of putting pressure on global supply chains, Dr. Ozcelic said.

Fawaz A. Gerges, a London School of Economics professor focusing on the Middle East, said the Houthis viewed the war with Iran as “a golden opportunity” to change the balance of power with Saudi Arabia in Yemen.

“Iran directly and indirectly benefits from what the Houthis have been doing,” he said, adding, “All-out war could have major implications for the global energy supply.”

Jenny Gross writes about business and economics for The Times and is based in London.

Lisa Friedman is a business correspondent covering energy for The New York Times.

Why Israel Reacted With Fury to U. K. Sanctions on West Bank Settlements

The New York Times September 09, 2026

Israel-Hamas Cease-Fire

Advertisement

Supported by

news analysis

The fierce retaliation of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government to the new restrictions is a reflection of his tough re-election fight, analysts say.

By David M. Halbfinger

Reporting from Jerusalem

When Britain announced sanctions on Tuesday against Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and said settlers there were taking part in the “ethnic cleansing” of Palestinians, the Israeli foreign minister accused his British counterpart of having acted for “domestic political reasons.”

The intensity of the Israeli response that followed could be chalked up to the exact same thing.

The foreign minister, Gideon Saar, lashed out at Ed Miliband, the British foreign secretary, in a news conference, saying his speech announcing the sanctions was based on “outrageous lies.” Mr. Saar ordered the swift closing of the British Consulate in Jerusalem, evicted British officials from an international center coordinating support for Gaza in southern Israel and barred from Israel a dozen British lawmakers and others he deemed anti-Israeli and antisemitic.

The robustness of that counterpunch cannot be disentangled from the fact that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government is up for re-election in less than seven weeks. In that sense, the British move may have played into the hands of the Israeli leader’s right-wing coalition, some analysts said.

Mr. Netanyahu, who was already on the defensive on a number of fronts and has struggled in the polls, has sought to wring political advantage from Israel’s military conflicts with several adversaries. He can now make the case to voters that the British diplomatic pressure is yet another reason to rally behind him.

“This is a government that relishes this idea that the world is against us,” said Alon Pinkas, a former Israeli diplomat and adviser to two of Mr. Netanyahu’s predecessors. “It’s a state of mind — that we’re the perpetual victim. And they think that they have to be the tough guy and show that we’re defiant and won’t succumb.”

Mr. Pinkas added that the ferocity of Mr. Saar’s response was an indication that Israel saw itself as fighting a rear-guard battle, especially after a dozen countries, including longtime allies like France and Canada, said on Tuesday that they supported the trade sanctions on the settlements.

“They are sensing a growing anti-Israeli tide all over the world, roughly since Oct. 7,” he said, “and they feel they have to stand up to it.”

Indeed, there is something of a competition underway within Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition cabinet to be the first and loudest to tell the rest of the world where it can go.

Itamar Ben-Gvir, the far-right security minister, who often stakes out extreme positions, publicly proposed that the government close the British Consulate in Jerusalem and seemed almost surprised when Mr. Saar went ahead and did it. Bezalel Smotrich, the far-right finance minister, went further and called for the British ambassador to be expelled.

Veteran Israeli diplomats said the government’s response also showed how far Israel had shifted away from even considering a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, after the British government said its sanctions were largely designed to help preserve the possibility of one.

Years ago, Israeli officials would almost certainly have argued that encouraging negotiations with the Palestinians was the best way forward, not taking unilateral retaliatory moves, said Jeremy Issacharoff, a career diplomat who retired as Israel’s ambassador to Germany.

Not so now. “Where’s the diplomacy?” he said. “It doesn’t exist.”

While Mr. Saar complained in his news conference of Britain’s “one-sided, anti-Israel approach,” he said nothing of talks with the Palestinians about a political solution to the conflict. Rather, he repeatedly said that the Israeli public rejected the creation of a Palestinian state in the West Bank and “overwhelmingly” supported settlements in the territory — though they are considered illegal by much of the world because international law bars an occupying power from moving its citizens into captured land. And Mr. Saar warned that no amount of international pressure could dislodge the settlements.

“We did not return to our land after 2,000 years only to lose it under pressure from jihadists, Islamists, antisemites, far-leftists and wokes,” Mr. Saar said.

To Mr. Issacharoff, the conclusion to be drawn from Mr. Saar’s response was simple and bleak.

“What he’s basically saying is we want a one-state reality in which we control the whole of the land of Israel,” he said. That would mean Israel either grants Palestinians equal rights and ceases to be a Jewish state, or denies them equality and ceases to be a democracy.

Some on Israel’s political left welcomed the aggressive new British policy.

“I strongly believe that the Miliband measures are good for Israel,” said Nadav Tamir, a former diplomat who heads the Israeli office of J Street, a pro-Israel lobbying group in the United States that supports a two-state solution. “Any move to prevent annexation and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank,” he said, would “help us to be more secure and more moral.”

But others said they feared there could be unintended consequences: The sanctions could aid Mr. Netanyahu’s re-election campaign, and Britain, an important ally of Israel, may have squandered any leverage it possessed.

Mr. Miliband could have explicitly offered to revisit the sanctions program if a new Israeli government was elected and it curbed illegal settlement expansions. Instead, he said only that Britain would “continue to assess the government of Israel” in hopes of seeing “a new approach.”

That could mean that a new Israeli leader would be unwilling to spend precious political capital taking on the pro-settlement community, even to a limited degree, analysts said.

“I think there could’ve been some carrot put on the table that, once Israeli policy changes for the better, these sanctions could be withdrawn,” Mr. Issacharoff said.

The fact that the British sanctions will not take effect for six to nine months leaves some room for flexibility, however.

For right-wing Israelis, the idea that the new British policy was meant to encourage a two-state solution was belied by what they saw as its one-sidedness. Mr. Miliband made only the briefest mention of the need for the Palestinian Authority, which administers part of the West Bank, to “accelerate reform,” for example, and said nothing about terrorist acts committed by Palestinians in the territory.

Alan Baker, a former Israeli ambassador to Canada, said Britain appeared to have thrown in so squarely with the Palestinians that it had lost any claim to impartiality.

“The feeling toward the British,” he said, “is that the British Mandate ended in 1948, and the time when the British were able to tell Israel what to do ended then, too.”

David M. Halbfinger is The Times’s Jerusalem bureau chief, leading coverage of Israel, Gaza and the West Bank. He also held that post from 2017 to 2021. He was the politics editor from 2021 to 2025.

By Eileen Sullivan and Adam Sella

Illustrations by Lily Boyce

Eileen Sullivan and Adam Sella reported from Washington, and Lily Boyce from New York.

The U. S. Postal Service is poised to play a critical new role in determining which mail ballots are delivered to voters this fall. If the Supreme Court allows President Trump to move forward with an executive order he issued in March, the agency would screen ballots after they are submitted by election officials and would deliver only those that comply with new rules. Two dozen states have sued to halt the plan, calling it unconstitutional.

Here’s how the process would work, according to notices issued by the Postal Service:

1

Each ballot envelope must:

Include the official Election Mail logo

Be able to be scanned by Postal Service machines

Bear each voter’s unique Postal Service bar code

Some states already voluntarily follow some of these guidelines. But for those that do not, redesigning ballot envelopes this late in the process and getting them approved by the Postal Service could be logistically challenging or impossible and cause delays, according to election officials.

2

VOTERS

The Postal Service will deliver mail ballots only to the voters on these lists.

Each list must include three key pieces of information for each voter:

Name

Address

Unique bar code

This adds a new step before mail ballots can go out. The chief election officer in each state is responsible for uploading lists in a standardized format or delegating that task to other officials. The portal is still under construction. The Postal Service has said it is expected to be ready soon for states to begin to voluntarily comply.

3

These bulk mailings can contain tens of thousands of ballots, often in plastic-wrapped pallets. The ballot envelopes must comply with the new design requirements and must have bar codes that match the list of approved mail voters that states submitted to the portal.

If a ballot envelope is not in compliance, the mailing will be rejected and returned to election officials. Election officials must address and fix any errors before resubmitting the mailing, which would delay the delivery of ballots to voters.

Eileen Sullivan is a Times reporter covering the changes to the federal work force under the Trump administration.

Adam Sella covers breaking news for The Times in Washington.

Missouri Supreme Court Sets Contempt Hearing in Fight Over House Map

The New York Times September 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Amid conflicting rulings, Missouri’s highest court ordered the secretary of state to respond to claims that he violated an order on redistricting.

By Mitch Smith

Intensifying a night of litigious chaos that spanned four courts, the fight over Missouri’s U. S. House districts has returned to the state’s Supreme Court, which signaled just before midnight Tuesday that it was considering whether to hold its top election officer in contempt.

The fight over which U. S. House districts will be used in November’s general election remained unsettled on Tuesday night after contradictory decisions from Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh of the U. S. Supreme Court and a federal district judge in St. Louis.

The State Supreme Court’s decision to call in Secretary of State Denny Hoskins for a contempt hearing, scheduled for Thursday morning, reflected a new juncture in a rising battle over what appears on Missouri ballots and over which judges’ orders should be heeded.

Mr. Hoskins and his fellow Republican officials said Tuesday night that they would keep using congressional districts redrawn last year at President Trump’s request to benefit Republicans, following the federal district judge’s order instead of the State Supreme Court’s.

“I look forward to my day in court,” Mr. Hoskins said in an overnight social media post that cited the supremacy clause of the U. S. Constitution.

The redrawn boundaries were used in last month’s primary election, but they were deemed invalid last week by the Missouri Supreme Court. The court’s order said that the previous lines must be used until a referendum was held on whether to switch to the redrawn districts.

Missouri officials warned of a constitutional breakdown and appealed that decision to the U. S. Supreme Court, but Justice Kavanaugh denied their appeal on Tuesday evening. For a moment, it seemed that the old boundaries would go back into effect, positioning Democrats to hold onto the Kansas City-area House seat that Republicans had hoped to flip.

But soon after Justice Kavanaugh’s decision was announced, word spread that a federal district judge in St. Louis had entered a conflicting order that instructed Mr. Hoskins to not change back to the old lines. Mr. Hoskins, along with Missouri’s governor and attorney general, quickly announced that they would follow the district judge’s ruling, setting off another round of frenzied court filings.

Opponents of the redrawn map immediately appealed the district judge’s ruling to the U. S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, which had taken no action as of early Wednesday morning. Those opponents also said that they would also ask Justice Kavanaugh, who oversees emergency requests from Missouri, to intervene.

Adding to the chaos, Tuesday was the deadline to finalize Missouri’s ballot. Several Missouri county clerks did not respond to interview requests on Tuesday night about the uncertainty.

The conflicting court orders followed a year of recriminations about Missouri’s congressional map. The state, which is led by Republicans, was among the first to join the redistricting arms race last year as Mr. Trump sought to boost his party’s odds of holding the House in the midterms.

By redrawing the lines outside the usual once-a-decade cycle, Missouri Republicans saw an opportunity to unseat one of the two Democrats in their state’s congressional delegation. State legislators passed the new map in a special session last September despite large protests and pleas from Democratic legislators.

In the months since, opponents of the new map have clashed repeatedly with Republican officials in court. The two sides have sparred over the legality of the redistricting effort, over the validity of a petition drive to force a statewide vote on the new lines, and over which court should have the final word on the boundaries.

After Mr. Hoskins said on Tuesday that he would forge ahead with using the redrawn boundaries — complying with the federal district judge’s order — redistricting opponents filed a motion seeking to have Mr. Hoskins held in contempt by the state’s high court.

“This court should make clear that regardless of other orders (except from the United States Supreme Court) the Missouri secretary of state must comply with this court’s injunction,” Charles W. Hatfield, a lawyer for the redistricting opponents, wrote in his motion with the State Supreme Court.

That court, which has five judges appointed by Republican governors and two appointed by Democrats, ruled unanimously against Mr. Hoskins last week.

Late on Tuesday night, Chief Justice W. Brent Powell scheduled a hearing on whether to hold Mr. Hoskins in contempt and instructed the secretary of state to appear in person.

The Missouri Supreme Court has called in Secretary of State Denny Hoskins for a contempt hearing for not following its order on which congressional map to use in November.

Chief Justice Powell, who was appointed by a Republican governor, also asked Mr. Hoskins to reply in writing on Wednesday to concerns about his instructions to county election officials and his willingness to abide by court rulings.

“Denny Hoskins is hereby ordered to show cause, if any, why he should not be held in contempt for violating this court’s injunction,” Chief Justice Powell wrote in the single-page order.

Earlier on Tuesday evening, Mr. Hoskins had praised the federal district’s judge ruling, which he said “halts a full-on constitutional crisis.”

“I am proud to lead this charge,” he added.

Ann E. Marimow contributed reporting.

Mitch Smith is a Chicago-based national correspondent for The Times, covering the Midwest and Great Plains.

What to Wear on Campus This Fall

The New York Times September 09, 2026

Advertisement

Newsletter

The host of The Fashions explains. And we share what you’re wearing.

By Matt Yan

I’m the host of Extra Credit, a newsletter for college students.

Good morning! It’s our second day of Back to School week. Today, we’re talking about what to wear on campus.

I wore some of my best (and worst) outfits in college. So I wanted to share some inspo with you, from my colleague who knows what’s up.

We’re also covering:

Your six talking points

Your fit checks (a reminder, send us your submissions here!)

And a former Dallas Cowboys cheerleader’s Broadway debut

What to know to be the smartest person in class today.

1. Iran is taking a more aggressive approach in the war. The country is concerned it’s losing control over the Strait of Hormuz.

2. Oil prices hit $100 a barrel. That’s nearly 40 percent higher than the price before the war with Iran.

3. The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to allow a voter-screening tool. The database would help spot ineligible voters ahead of the midterm elections, the administration said. But voting rights groups said it could disenfranchise voters.

4. OpenAI chatbots solved a major math problem: It’s what mathematicians call “the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem,” which involves a series of equations that are often used to predict the weather. The solution only took 88 hours.

5. Three jurors described what happened in the Lindsay Clancy mistrial. Read more details from inside their tense deliberations.

6. Ben Shelton beat Carlos Alcaraz in the latest end to a match in U. S. Open history. The match ended after five sets at 3:33 a. m. Shelton will face a fellow American, Frances Tiafoe, tomorrow.

It’s Jacob Gallagher’s job to know what’s cool. He hosts The Fashions, a newsletter that covers trends and what’s on the runway. (He once did a knee reveal for his readers.)

College quads can sometimes feel like catwalks. Students show off their personal style, some for the first time after years in high school uniforms.

If you want to look your best, Jacob has some advice. This conversation has been edited.

Matt: Jacob, what are your tips for putting together an outfit?

Jacob: I tend to start with one item of clothing that I really want to wear that day — maybe it’s a shirt I haven’t worn in a while or a sweater that feels calibrated just right for early fall — and I build from there. OK, what pants go with this, what shoes sit right. It’s the Lego approach. You build brick by brick.

I also always try to find balance between uptight and casual. If I’m wearing more traddy, pleated wool pants, maybe I’ll dilute that dressiness with some flat-soled sneakers or a more graphic sweater. Or if I really just want to wear something insouciant like a polo, then I’ll make sure I have loafers on as a more polished foundation.

If you were a college student today, what would you wear?

It’s so subjective! I think it really depends on what you’re trying to achieve. Are you trying to fit in or be taken more seriously? As an outsider who is now well more than a decade removed from campus life, I tend to think a smidge of polish can do a lot. Does it make me washed and unc to, say … wear a button-up instead of a tee? Jeans instead of sweats? Maybe black loafers instead of Sambas?

What were you actually wearing as a college student?

Oh, god. What a question. Early in college, I wore a pair of Sperry Topsiders that were so battered and abused (and, to be honest, beer-stained) that I should’ve donated them to science. I wore characterless jeans and a lot of button-down shirts. Always cotton — I liked the stiffness — rather than poly.

For the back half of college, I moved to New York, and I started working at clothing stores, so I actually started wearing a lot of blazers, dress pants and brogues. It was maybe too much for class.

If you had to choose one staple item, what would it be?

Again, get some good cotton shirts. They’re the kind of thing you can thrift or buy for under $50 at Uniqlo, and they’ll serve you well. You’ll need them for interviews, but you can also chuck them over some shorts on the weekend. Easiest, most versatile thing you can have in the closet.

How has fashion changed on campuses?

I do think postpandemic everything (and this is not just on the campus) became way more dressed-down. There used to be a certain sense of “getting dressed up” for class that I think just doesn’t really exist anymore.

What trends are you seeing among college students and Gen Z?

There is a lot of talk right now about how young people dress in this placeless, context-free mishmash. We call it “Gen Z chaos” on our desk. When I was in college, your clothes reflected who you were, what you were into, what music you liked, what hobbies you had. I think you can’t really look at someone and glean that info anymore. There’s a lot of cobbling together thrifted clothes, stuff you’ve bought off TikTok Shop, making a shirt you inherited from a sibling into something that looks, well, interesting, perhaps rather than good. (Sorry!)

Here are tips on layering, wearing oversize clothing and picking colors.

Nursing students at New York University sent me their outfits. Send me yours here.

Hillary Leger, 21, nursing and global public health student

The details: This was my first-day-of-school outfit in my third year of nursing school. I wanted to look as good as all the effort I’d put in all semester. I’d like to think it worked because I passed all my exams.

The occasion: First-day lectures.

Anything else? If you look good, you feel good and perform better.

Tenneh Sandimanie, 28, nursing student

The details: I’ve been loving jorts and grunge acid-wash color palettes lately.

The occasion: Dinner with friends.

Julia Reid Adelan, 23, nursing student

The reasoning: Making the most of the last bits of summer before it gets colder!

The occasion: Happy hour, and exploring the West Village.

I loved these photos of Juilliard students with members of the New York Philharmonic. (Vogue)

The stories you should read before they hit the group chat.

A former Dallas Cowboys cheerleader is making her Broadway debut. Reece Weaver, a breakout star on Netflix’s “America’s Sweethearts,” is playing Roxie Hart in “Chicago.” This comes after the show found success casting an influencer, Whitney Leavitt of “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives,” in the role.

It’s the summer of new TV shows portraying female friendship. The creators of “Sterling Point” and “Off Campus” are focused on supportive — not competitive — friendships.

Do this to get ahead.

Read a new novel. Try one of these 35 coming out this fall.

Spice up your workout routine. One of these exercises could make you look better lifting than everyone else. (Do you have a fancy campus gym? Tell me the details.)

Make a playlist for the fall, and add these good new songs to it. I just made a fall list called “hopecore.”

Thanks for hanging out with me this morning. This newsletter is powered by your submissions — tell us about your classes, questions, crushes, side hustles and obsessions here.

Also: Times access is free for half of all U. S. college students through their school. Tell your friends to check if their school provides free access.

And forward this to your roommate, professor, club president or T. A. See you tomorrow!

P. S. Want to know about the rebrand of this newsletter? Read an interview about it here.

Want more of today’s top stories? Tune in to “The Headlines,” our podcast that covers the biggest news of the day. It’s short, like our news recap.

Any tips or feedback? I’m all ears. Email me at extracredit@nytimes. com

The editor of Extra Credit is Lauren Jackson. Will Baxter was our photo editor.

Connections Coach

The 9/11 completist community wants to know and see everything. The Holy Grail? Pictures from inside the twin towers.

Jonathan Walczak was only 13 in 2001, yet he has devoted himself to impartially documenting the attacks on Sept. 11. Credit... Ruth Fremson/The New York Times

Supported by

By Michael Wilson

Michael Wilson reported this story from New York and Indiana.

When he was 15 years old, Jonathan Walczak came upon a newspaper article that described a disposable camera found in the pocket of a dead man in the rubble of the World Trade Center.

An F. B. I. agent quoted in that 2003 article said his team had developed the film from the camera, revealing pictures taken from inside one of the towers as the Sept. 11 attacks were unfolding.

Jonathan had been to the twin towers, once, with his grandparents and his younger brother when he was little. He read to the end of the article, then he read it again and clipped it out. The description of those photos cast a spell on him that he could not shake. An extremely specific fixation took root.

Years passed. Mr. Walczak graduated from college in North Carolina and became a newspaper reporter before moving to Manhattan in 2010 to attend graduate school. He lasted only one semester, but that fall in the city triggered memories. He watched the ninth anniversary of the terror attacks, and thought about that camera. He had kept the newspaper clipping all those years. Where was the camera now? Could he see those pictures? They sounded so vivid.

His time as a reporter taught him how to access government documents. Later that year, Mr. Walczak, now in his early 20s, filed a request under the Freedom of Information Act — his first of many — demanding that the F. B. I. release the pictures from that disposable camera.

“There is no other camera like this,” he wrote in his request. “There are no other photos like these.”

Mr. Walczak is quick to clarify something at this point in conversations about the missing film. He does not believe the pictures will reveal some hidden explanation for the events of that day. He is not a conspiracy theorist.

He is something different — a Sept. 11 completist. The two can look very similar from a distance, people foraging for things that will supposedly show what really happened on that day. But Mr. Walczak has a track record of actually finding them.

On an episode of a 2021 podcast he created, “Missing on 9/11,” he rattled off a list of photos that he has verified were taken on various floors of the towers: “One picture from the 48th, three from the 35th, one from the 51st, five from the 74th, two from the 61st.”

And in his sprawling, labyrinthine quest for those photographs, he would come to know a community of sleuths intent on finding and preserving unseen footage from that singular day. They huddle in Reddit threads, inspecting images and triangulating the exact positions of the photographers.

“People just assume everything’s been published,” Mr. Walczak said. “Not only is that not true, there’s a lot of fascinating footage that hasn’t been published.”

It is like they are working together on a puzzle that, 25 years later, still seems not quite complete. And new pieces keep emerging.

Just this year, amateur Sept. 11 archivists have found a gripping video from a forgotten Camcorder, and another showing office equipment falling from the highest floors — likely thrown through the reinforced glass windows by people desperate for fresh air. These are marked within the community as major discoveries.

But for Mr. Walczak, the disposable camera remains the big one.

The story that the teenage Jonathan Walczak clipped out was written by a Baltimore Sun reporter named Laura Sullivan. In 2003, she spent time with the F. B. I. Explosives Unit at its storage facility in Quantico, Va., a main repository for evidence from Sept. 11.

Deep in the article, her focus turned to the disposable camera. Mr. Walczak has reread those sentences countless times, analyzing them for clues about the photographer or the people around him that day.

“Unit members found a disposable camera in the pocket of a man who jumped from one of the towers,” Ms. Sullivan wrote. “When they developed the film months later, investigators found a chilling chronology of the man’s experience that morning.”

“The photos show the man, who appears to be a construction worker, standing at the window as the other tower burns behind him. The photos, which include pictures he took as well as a few taken by someone else, also capture other jumpers falling. The man looks stricken, his face one of shock and disbelief.”

There were solid clues to chase down. Construction worker … the photo taken as the other tower burns.

The specificity of this description intrigued him. Many articles, books, documentaries and films have been made about that morning in Manhattan. One would imagine that there’s nothing new. But relatively few images from inside the towers have been seen. And none are known to have surfaced from the floors above where the planes hit.

He sought to convey the significance of the photos in his podcast in 2021.

“To me, they’re the Zapruder film of 9/11,” he said. “They’re singular and unique, a point of view unlike any other, documenting a monumental moment in American history.”

But time after time, in his view, he was stonewalled by the F. B. I.

He pursued other avenues. During the “Missing on 9/11” podcast, he made a bonus episode, “The Disposable Camera.” And he invited a guest: the reporter who wrote the Sun story 18 years earlier.

“I email you out of the blue,” Mr. Walczak reminded the reporter, Ms. Sullivan, by then with National Public Radio. “Did you kind of wonder what this is about?”

“I was like, ‘Oh, my God, what did I write?’” she replied. “‘What did I do now?’” But she remembered that day in the Quantico evidence lab.

“I had a flash of Mohamed Atta’s suitcase,” she told Mr. Walczak. “And then it all came rushing back.”

In the evidence room that day in 2003, a brand-new suitcase rested on a table. It belonged to Mr. Atta, a hijacker who struck the north tower — luggage checked so as to avoid drawing suspicion as a passenger with no bags. The suitcase missed the connecting Flight 11 in Boston from Portland, Maine, and thus survived.

She vaguely remembered the photos. Mostly, she remembers the feelings they evoked.

“It was a man in a beige outfit standing by a window,” she told him. “It was sort of the emotional pull of them, that they were taken in this moment of tragedy.”

The pictures seemed to reveal, she said, “this moment that was his last moment — that he didn’t really know it was his last moment.”

Five years after that podcast, Ms. Sullivan can still recall how she felt about the people in the photographs. “Something about them,” she said, “felt trapped.”

She understands the allure of analog found footage.

“In this day and age, we want to be reminded of what’s real,” she said. “An image from that morning of a person living that nightmare, that’s real. And from a disposable camera — it’s real in a way that images today are not.”

As Mr. Walczak dug deeper into the footage from Sept. 11, someone suggested he reach out to a younger man who was regarded as something of an expert. His name was Andrew Boston. Mr. Walczak was skeptical — Mr. Boston was an electrician in his 20s in Nebraska. But he gave him a call.

His doubts vanished: “We spoke for three or four hours.”

Mr. Boston was only 5 years old on Sept. 11, but he remembers it for a specific fright. His father was away on business on the East Coast, and was supposed to fly home that day, but no one had heard from him. His worried mother basically ignored him, and he sat in front of a television showing the scene from Manhattan.

“I do recall the south tower collapse, watching at home,” Mr. Boston says now. “After that my brother and I were sent into the basement, and we played Nintendo. I think my most ever-present thought was, ‘Something very bad is happening.’”

As the afternoon dragged on, the boy ended up on the porch with his mother. Neighbors were outside, too. Then, as Mr. Boston remembers today, there was a tremendous roar overhead. Everyone looked up — it was a huge jet.

“I could see every panel,” Mr. Boston said. A grown-up explained what it was: Air Force One, the president’s plane.

During the chaos that day, Air Force One darted around the country, from Florida to Louisiana to Offutt Air Force Base in Nebraska — a few miles from the Boston family’s house.

And a few hours later, Mr. Boston’s father called home — he was safe, his plane diverted to a small airfield.

“It was the first big event of my life,” Mr. Boston, now 30, said. “Every generation has that something that you become aware, ‘Oh, there’s a bigger world than what’s going on around me.’”

To come of age after the attacks is to grow up seeing images from that day. “Wherever you look, documentaries, books — there was always a new thing to learn,” he said.

It followed him into adulthood, where he discovered false claims about what happened that day. “People were, like, just making stuff up,” he said. “This is just bad history.”

Two or three years ago, he began devoting serious time to collecting and cataloging Sept. 11 footage, helping build a community on Reddit called r/911archive. He wanted, for example, to understand — in granular detail — what caused the buildings to collapse. He has sought to understand why some escape routes were available while others were not. He has examined the role of vertical shafts and voids in the collapse.

“It’s a disservice to not try to understand why,” he explained. “It’s history that gets lost.”

The community is still finding footage. Just last year, a newly discovered videocassette — a harrowing scene recorded by a contractor named Edward Sferrazza — was digitized and posted online. It begins with people staring up at one burning building, then a second, and finally, suddenly, everyone is engulfed by ash. Mr. Sferrazza, gasping for air, returns to his van to find two strangers inside, seeking refuge.

“That was huge,” Mr. Boston said of the video. “I’ve never seen something so visceral and so human.”

For his part, Mr. Sferrazza, the contractor, said last week in an interview that he hasn’t watched and has no intention to. He released the video for the sole purpose of rebutting Sept. 11 deniers, he said.

“I just want it to be known that, when they compare it to the moon landing, I was there,” he said. “I smelled it, I tasted it, I lived it.”

Mr. Walczak, though, was not making any progress whatsoever in his search for the disposable rubble camera. Time after time, his Freedom of Information Act requests to the F. B. I. were denied. His description of the material he sought was always too vague, the bureau said.

After having sent more than two dozen requests for documents over 15 years, adding new search terms or names of construction workers who perished, Mr. Walczak finally sued the bureau in federal court last year. He accused the agency of, in effect, not looking hard enough. That lawsuit is playing out in the Southern District of New York, but he felt as if he was nearing a dead end.

There was one more obvious person to contact: the F. B. I. agent who ran the evidence lab in Quantico and who showed the pictures to Ms. Sullivan in 2003.

His name was Donald Sachtleben, and in 2003, he was approaching the end of a remarkable career as a bomb technician — a career that, in the years to follow, would itself implode in spectacular fashion.

His dangerous outings, and the toll they took, are described in detailed court documents.

Mr. Sachtleben, then an agent in his early 30s, gathered evidence in New York after terrorists bombed the World Trade Center in 1993. Impressed with his work, the F. B. I. flew him to Oklahoma City the day Timothy McVeigh detonated a truck bomb at the Federal Building, killing 168. He spent weeks there, picking through corpses for evidence, and after dark, drinking the day’s horrors away in bars.

In 1996, during the Unabomber investigation, agents zeroed in on a suspect: Ted Kaczynski, a recluse who lived in a tiny cabin in the Montana woods. Mr. Sachtleben entered the cabin after Mr. Kaczynski’s arrest, and he found a live bomb under the bed. And it was Mr. Sachtleben — “too stupid to be afraid,” he would say later — who drove the bulldozer carrying the explosives down an icy hill to a spot where the bomb could be safely detonated.

After the attacks of 2001, Mr. Sachtleben worked on the ground in Shanksville, Pa., the scene of the crashed Flight 93. He listened to the black box recording of the passengers wresting control of the plane from the terrorists. “The psychological and emotional toll that work took on Don was enormous,” his lawyers would later state.

He left the F. B. I. in 2008, then returned as a contractor with full access to top secret information. But four years later, investigators made a disturbing discovery when they searched his laptop: He was storing and sharing child sexual abuse imagery. A separate investigation revealed that Mr. Sachtleben had also leaked secret information about a failed bomb plot to the media.

He was arrested and charged in both cases, and pleaded guilty in both. His lawyers said the burnout from his stressful career and heavy drinking led him to use poor judgment. He spent nine years in prison.

During that time, Mr. Walczak tracked him down and wrote to him, asking about the photos from the disposable camera.

Can’t help you, Mr. Sachtleben replied. “There were hundreds of thousands of photos related to the 9/11 investigation,” he wrote from prison. “I imagine these images are tucked away in some storage bin.”

Mr. Sachtleben was released in 2022. Today, he lives far from his old life, in a house at the end of a quiet cul-de-sac near a stocked fishing pond in rural Indiana. Mr. Walczak wrote him here, too, and received the same reply. Can’t help.

When a reporter visited the former agent in August, Mr. Sachtleben listened quietly to questions about the disposable camera and the pictures it yielded.

“I cannot be part of this story,” he said in a brief conversation. He was not allowed to discuss F. B. I. matters without approval, he said.

Asked if he simply remembered the photos, he said: “Somewhat.”

Earlier this year, a head of the F. B. I.’s Record/Information Dissemination Section filed a detailed court response to Mr. Walczak’s lawsuit, outlining the lengths to which the bureau has gone to find this camera. The bureau tried dozens of terms — “disposable,” “rubble,” “camera,” “pocket,” “jumper,” “tower” — in internal search engines, to no avail.

The storage area the Sun reporter had visited is now a mail room, and the evidence that was held there has been transferred elsewhere. Several offices were physically searched in recent months for any sign of the camera or photographs, the F. B. I. said. No luck.

As his search for the camera plods on, Mr. Walczak has become an expert on other so-called rubble cameras found in the ruins of ground zero. Those investigations have proved more fruitful.

He took a deep dive into the contents of a professional-grade camera found at ground zero, and sought to identify its owner by reaching out to the people photographed in the chaotic minutes after the towers were struck. He studied shadows cast by buildings to determine exactly what time different pictures were taken.

He turned that investigation into a documentary called “32 Frames: A 9/11 Mystery.” It arrived on streaming platforms this month.

He gets one question a lot. So does his friend Mr. Boston. So do all the Sept. 11 completists.

Why?

“I turned 13 three days before 9/11,” Mr. Walczak said. “It was a coming-of-age moment for me.” The event shook him. And to find community and purpose in revisiting that time after so long — to realize he wasn’t alone in wanting to learn more — is something like a nice surprise.

“These people really deeply care,” he said. “It’s a community of young people who were impacted as kids by 9/11, who the torch has been passed to.”

The attacks immediately sent him back to the day in 2000, visiting the towers with his grandparents as an 11-year-old. I was just there, he thought with wonder on Sept. 11, elevating that day to a core memory. In the same way, Mr. Boston in Nebraska recalls sitting helplessly on his porch, hoping his father was somewhere safe, when the president flew over his house.

Twenty-five years on, they keep coming back to those moments, to that day. Still looking for pieces of a puzzle that the world handed them when they were boys.

I love meandering, twisty quests, and this one sounded like it fit the bill — hunting for a dead man’s disposable camera, last seen at an F. B. I. evidence storage unit in 2003. And along the way, I met young, amateur investigators who know as much about the fallen World Trade Center as some experts, and yet never set foot in the towers.

Michael Wilson, who covers New York City, has been a Times reporter for more than two decades.

Texas Republicans Are Turning Against Data Centers. Will It Matter in November?

The New York Times September 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The industry’s rapid expansion has scrambled traditional political alliances and forced G. O. P. leaders to respond to a backlash from some of their most reliable rural voters.

By J. David GoodmanRebecca F. Elliott and Brad Plumer

J. David Goodman reported from Hillsboro, Hubbard and Houston, Texas. Rebecca F. Elliott reported from New York and Brad Plumer from Washington.

Construction trucks bound for a data center site near Hillsboro, Texas, clattered through the town square on a recent morning, drowning out conversation and tossing dust onto the outdoor tables of Kelley and Michael Ivy’s burger restaurant.

“People can’t even sit outside,” Ms. Ivy said, watching the seemingly nonstop caravan.

“They’re ruining the beautiful countryside,” Mr. Ivy added.

Both longtime Republican voters, the couple opposed the nearby construction, southwest of Dallas, because of concerns about its impact on the landscape and local water systems. They blamed Republican state leaders, like Gov. Greg Abbott, who they felt had allowed the data center industry’s headlong expansion. They wanted a change.

Would they vote for a Democrat in the fall? Neither said they would.

“It’s one of those things I pray about,” Ms. Ivy said. “What do you do?”

The rush of data center construction has fueled a potent bipartisan backlash across the country this year, creating unusual political alliances ahead of the November midterms. Democrats hope the anger will weaken Republicans among some of their most reliable rural voters. Republicans are betting that although those voters may dislike data centers, they are not ready to abandon the party over them.

The stakes are particularly high in Texas, home to more data centers than any other state except Virginia and where Republicans face the biggest political threat to their statewide dominance in years.

It is hard to overstate how important Texas is to the tech industry, whose growth depends heavily on building data centers in a state that, until recently, made such development relatively easy. Late last year, Mr. Abbott crowned Texas the “epicenter of A. I. development.” Up to half of the nation’s new data center capacity predicted from 2027 through 2030 is expected to be built in the state, according to Jefferies, an investment bank.

Then last month, Mr. Abbott abruptly called for a pause on connecting hundreds of large data centers to the state’s power grid until the projects underwent a full audit of their local impacts, including energy and water use. That process is likely to stretch beyond the election in November.

Public backlash against data centers has also extended to energy projects in Texas, imperiling longtime plans to build high-voltage transmission lines across the state. Without new transmission lines, the Permian Basin — home to the Texas oil industry — is at risk of rolling blackouts, according to the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, the grid manager.

Mr. Abbott’s decision last month to seek a pause on new data centers was a sign of just how fraught the politics have become for Republicans. Many of their own voters have turned against the projects. Some have even joined with Democrats to fight them.

“Hey guys, it’s OK, we can work with Democrats,” said Elena Voytko, a conservative Christian who has been an outspoken opponent of data centers in Temple, Texas.

At the same time, Ms. Voytko said finding common cause with Democrats on data centers had not changed how she planned to vote.

“They are bringing in data centers,” she said of Republican leaders. “But if we bring in Democrats, they’re going to not only change the fabric of Temple and Bell County, but of the whole state.”

Democrats hope the anger over data centers will dampen Republican turnout and even push some voters their way. They have seized on comments from President Trump, including his remark on Monday that communities that oppose data centers “want to end up being backwards and poor.”

For Republicans, the bet is that the issue, while important to those who live near the enormous construction sites, will not motivate enough average voters.

A recent survey from the University of Texas at Austin found Republicans split on the issue, even when asked about data centers in their own communities, while independents and Democrats were decisively against.

But only about a quarter of voters in rural areas supported data centers in the survey — a potential warning sign for Republicans who rely on turnout in these communities to overcome the advantage Democrats have in Texas cities.

“It’s an issue that just isn’t bubbling up as a top concern yet,” said Dave Carney, Mr. Abbott’s top political strategist. Voters do not rank data centers ahead of the economy or cost of living, he said. “But you say, ‘What do you think about data centers?’ They say, ‘Oh, they suck.’”

Still, Democrats want to capitalize on what they perceive as an advantage. Gina Hinojosa, who is challenging Mr. Abbott, has called for an immediate moratorium on data center projects. James Talarico, the party’s nominee for U. S. Senate, has called for tighter regulation.

Republicans face a particular challenge because their party has long supported the industry, said Sid Miller, the Republican agriculture commissioner who has sparred publicly with Mr. Abbott.

“The Democrats, they’re right on the issue,” Mr. Miller said. “We’re going to lose some seats over this.”

For months, anger among residents of rural Hill County — which favored President Trump 82 to 18 in 2024 — has grown over the data center projects popping up around the area. County leaders, frustrated by their inability to do anything on their own, looked to the state for guidance, said Judge Shane Brassell, the county’s top executive. They received none.

So the county issued its own one-year moratorium on data center construction. Some Republican politicians, including State Senator Paul Bettencourt of Houston, quickly said the county had no power to do so. One of the data center companies filed suit, personally naming Judge Brassell and other county leaders. The county quickly rescinded its moratorium.

“One of the ultimate goals was trying to get the state to become involved,” Judge Brassell said, seated in his office at the Hill County courthouse.

Mr. Bettencourt said the State Legislature would take up the issue in its session next year. “There’s clearly going to be top-down regulations from the state,” he said.

In a telephone interview, Mr. Bettencourt stopped short of criticizing data center development broadly.

“I’m not going to say that data centers are bad because they’re literally being used right now to support our phone call,” he said. He added that the 2026 election was the “frothiest” he had ever seen.

Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is running for U. S. Senate, has also sought to address the backlash, unveiling his own plan for data centers last month. He said he supported Mr. Abbott’s pause and, if elected, would introduce federal legislation to make data center companies criminally liable for “A. I. chatbots that undermine children’s safety.”

Part of the challenge for Republicans is that some of their own voters do not believe the proposed changes will halt the industry in Texas.

Despite Mr. Abbott’s pause on grid approvals, many data center projects are still moving forward with construction in the meantime. The pause also won’t affect companies planning to generate their own power off-grid.

Allison Clements, a former member of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, is among those who see the pause on new data center permit approvals as a temporary delay, rather than a step toward banning new projects. (New York, in July, became the first state to enact a moratorium on data center development.)

“There is so much significant development going on in Texas for the governor to single-handedly turn off the switch,” Ms. Clements said. “It’s almost unthinkable.”

Publicly, many tech and power companies have supported Texas’ new data center review process. Few can afford to alienate the governor of a state so critical to their growth plans.

“As far as timing goes, Texas is a get-things-done state,” Robert J. Gaudette, chief executive of Houston-based power company NRG Energy, told Wall Street analysts in August. “I expect them to work through stuff to get to a higher quality understanding of the projects.”

In Hubbard, Texas, last week, trucks formed a steady line of traffic en route to the sprawling site of a particularly large data center under construction outside town.

Jennifer Gentry, 56, moved to Hubbard several years ago. It was a quintessential small Texas town with parades on holidays and an old Victorian home that she had long admired. The arrival of the data center had changed all that, she said.

First came the boomtown feel of the construction: the noise, the traffic, the lights at night. Even after its completion, she feared, the town would be “something else,” never the same again. She is preparing to put her home on the market.

“They allowed it to happen,” Ms. Gentry, a Republican voter, said of Mr. Abbott and other state leaders. “They allowed them in, and they didn’t protect us.” She said the changes he proposed were “too late.”

Still, she said, she would probably not vote for any Democrats in the fall. She felt Democrats had “sold America out” when it came to immigration.

“With the Republicans, at least I know what I’m getting,” she said. “Even if it is something I don’t agree with.”

J. David Goodman is the Texas bureau chief for The Times, based in Houston.

Rebecca F. Elliott covers energy for The Times.

Brad Plumer is a Times reporter who covers technology and policy efforts to address global warming.

San Francisco Orders Meta to Stop ‘Allowing’ AI Child Abuse Ads

Wired September 09, 2026

San Francisco’s city attorney has hit Meta with a cease-and-desist letter telling the company to stop “allowing” paid advertisements that include AI-generated child sexual abuse content and asked it to explain how the ads repeatedly ran on its platforms.

On Tuesday, WIRED reported that Meta has run more than 350 ads in recent months that transformed still images of minors—some of them confirmed as real individuals, including a member of a European royal family—into short videoclips that can depict them performing sexual acts. When clicked, these ads would direct people to download AI image- and video-generation apps, some of which could be used to digitally undress people or create other nonconsensual intimate imagery.

The ads, which were discovered by researchers at the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), included some identical ads that had been uploaded multiple times, and in total they reached more than 29,000 accounts in countries in the European Union. The ads that were shown across Facebook, Instagram, and Threads also targeted accounts in the US, Australia, and India. WIRED initially reported on a batch of 53 of the ads at the start of August, but more than 250 of the total number of ads ran on Meta’s platforms after this initial report.

“Meta has failed to address a known issue of AI-generated child sexually explicit ads, while profiting from them," San Francisco city attorney David Chiu says in a statement to WIRED. “These ads are deeply disturbing and cause harm to real children. Meta claims to have zero tolerance for child exploitation, yet the scale and persistence of these issues suggest current efforts are woefully inadequate. This is unacceptable, and Meta must do better.”

“No company—particularly one that claims all advertisements are reviewed and approved prior to distribution and then accepts payment for that distribution—should permit its advertising systems to be used in this manner,” Chiu writes in the four-page letter his office sent to Meta’s lawyers.

The letter raises a host of questions about how Meta’s ad policies and safety systems operate and asks that the company’s legal, child-safety, and advertising staff engage in “prompt discussions” with the city office. “These findings are especially troubling because they do not appear to reflect an isolated failure that Meta corrected when first alerted to the problem,” Chiu writes.

Meta says there is “no indication” that the ads were displayed in San Francisco and this means they are “outside the city attorney's jurisdiction.” While Meta’s ad library, which is a repository of ads, includes some data about ads published in the US, it does not break down where in the US ads may have run.

In response to Meta's jurisdictional claims, City Attorney's Office spokesperson Alex Barrett-Shorter tells WIRED that, because “San Francisco consumers can access the unlawful ads through Meta online spaces,” the matter is the the city of San Francisco's business.

“We find Meta’s response astonishing. Meta appears less concerned about whether they’re guilty of exploiting children than whether San Francisco should say anything about it,” Barrett-Shorter says. “Meta has bigger problems to solve here than determining our jurisdiction.”

Meta previously told WIRED that many of the ads identified by the TTP researchers had already been removed before they were reported—all of them have now been removed for violating its policies—and most had “fewer than 200 impressions” from accounts. “We don’t tolerate nudify apps or any kind of child exploitation, whether real or AI-generated,” a Meta spokesperson previously said. The company said the “total ad spend” for the 300-plus ads found by the researchers was “under $5,000.”

The letter, which says the City Attorney’s Office has reviewed many of the ads found by the TTP researchers, demands that Meta stop the ads from running on its platforms and explain how the ads managed to avoid its moderation systems and how it escalates and reports ads to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and asks the company to detail how it addresses the advertisers behind the content and repeat offenders.

The letter continues to say the findings suggest “broader systemic problems” with how the company detects potential child sexual abuse in advertising and that it raises “significant legal questions” for the company. “My Office’s objective is not simply to identify past failures but to ensure that Meta puts systems in place that prevent children from being sexually exploited through advertisements Meta is paid to distribute, and that Meta reliably satisfies the legal obligations that arise when it becomes aware of apparent child sexual exploitation,” Chiu writes in the letter.

The findings from the TTP researchers stated that in some cases Meta did not respond to reports the agency made about abusive ads for more than a week, during which the ads were seen by hundreds more people. When some ads were removed, they were initially not marked as containing child sexual abuse content, according to TTP and a WIRED review of Meta’s ad library. “The scale, persistence, and nature of the problems documented here suggest that Meta’s isolated takedown efforts are woefully inadequate,” the letter from Chiu says, requesting Meta provide a response within 28 days.

Meta’s community standards and advertising policies do not allow child sexual exploitation, abuse, or nudity, nor adult exploitation or adult nudity. The company also does not allow the promotion of nudify apps. Meta’s ad standards say that all advertisements are reviewed against its policies using automated, and sometimes manual, reviews. The company has previously removed hundreds of thousands of ads for nudify apps.

Despite Meta taking action against nudify apps, including suing a Hong Kong–based company linked to one set of nudifier platforms and working with other tech companies, researchers continue to find thousands of ads that direct people to the harmful apps and that contain sexual activity and nudity. During WIRED’s reporting on the Tech Transparency Project findings, we identified hundreds of “nudification” ads currently running across Meta’s platforms.

Katie Paul, the director of TTP, says that Meta is “not effectively” addressing the issue, and ads containing child sexual abuse are still appearing on its plaform as of Wednesday. “Meta has claimed it takes a hard stance against child sexual abuse material, but since TTP’s September 8 report published, more brand-new ads have run featuring some of the same children TTP sent to Meta,” Paul says. The organization has reported the ads to Meta and the NCMEC and noted that some had already been removed. Meta did not immediately respond to WIRED’s question about new ads still appearing.

“The findings are clear,” Paul adds. “Meta is not effectively addressing this issue.”

Updated 9/9/2026 at 6 pm ET: Added additional comment from the San Francisco City Attorney's Office.

A Year After Charlie Kirk's Death, Turning Point Plans to Spend Big on the Midterms

Wired September 09, 2026

A year after the assassination of cofounder Charlie Kirk, Turning Point plans to pour tens of millions of dollars into the midterm elections to help Republican candidates in key congressional and gubernatorial races, according to sources familiar with the matter.

The conservative grassroots group is expected to prioritize three states in the midterms—New Hampshire, Arizona, and Nevada—but will also deploy full-time field staff in seven other states where Democrats could pick up seats.

The precise amounts could change, but sources tell WIRED that Turning Point's super PAC is looking to spend $15–$20 million in ads across the three priority states. Turning Point's field operation spending couldn't be learned, as it is run by a 501(c)(4) nonprofit, but it is estimated to be tens of millions more.

The planned cash injection will pay for both a field operation as well as digital ads, and would only add to the advantage for Republicans in funding through a constellation of outside super PACs and party committees.

The most closely watched race for Republicans in New Hampshire is the Senate seat vacated by the retiring Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, where former Republican senator John Sununu is running against Democratic representative Chris Pappas to flip the seat.

The New Hampshire Senate race is a crucial battleground for both parties, as many of the possible paths to Democrats taking the Senate majority require the party to keep the seat, which the Cook Political Report rates as "Lean Democrat."

Turning Point has also been particularly focused on the race for governor in Arizona, where Democratic incumbent Katie Hobbs is running against Representative Andy Biggs, who endorsed President Donald Trump's claims of a stolen election in 2020.

These maneuvers come as Republican groups have started a massive cash injection to counter a wave of discontent from voters over the Iran war and high prices, and burgeoning Democratic momentum that has opened up the possibility of a Democrat-controlled Senate.

After facing criticism for not spending earlier, Trump’s political operation has stepped into gear recently with a $10 million ad spend in the Texas Senate race through Trump’s main super PAC, MAGA Inc. More recently, Trump’s team has used No Going Back PAC Inc, a new entity, to reserve at least $47 million in ads in six Senate races and one House race.

The extent of the coordination between Trump's operation and MAGA Inc. with outside groups like Turning Point isn’t entirely clear, but there has been extensive data sharing to coordinate on which voters to reach, one of the sources said.

And with the midterms in November widely expected to be decided in part by turnout, Turning Point has communicated to Trump's orbit that a major focus of its field operation is reminding Trump supporters to actually vote on Election Day.

Unlike other super PACs, Turning Point has been an organization focused on presidential elections, and its midterm strategy is really an effort to build up infrastructure for the Republican ticket in 2028, the sources said.

The focus on New Hampshire, Arizona, and Nevada comes as Turning Point contends with the fact that winning those states in 2028 would offset Vice President JD Vance—or anyone else—needing to win traditional so-called blue-wall states.

You know what they say: The day after midterms is the first day of the presidential election. Republicans are already campaigning.

With Trump's approval rating now consistently at or under 40 percent, a historically dangerous level for a midterm election, Republicans have faced a dilemma over participating in the Republican "midterm convention" this week in Texas.

While party conventions are typically only held in presidential election years, Trump and other officials are set to headline the event in an effort to boost vulnerable Republicans like Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton and mobilize the base.

But by appearing with the president, Republicans in close races run the risk of being associated too closely with the political baggage of the Iran war as well as the higher gas and grocery prices that have resulted from the conflict.

As a way to partially offset the disincentives, the Republican National Committee has placed a heavy emphasis on using the convention to help fundraise on behalf of candidates who travel to Dallas, two Republican strategist sources tell Inner Loop.

On September 9, Trump will appear at what has been billed as a special RNC event. To attend a roundtable with Trump, donors will have to pay $250,000 per person. A photo opportunity with the president is $88,600 per photo.

On September 10, Vance will do his own RNC roundtable, where seats cost $75,000 per person. A photo with the vice president will cost $35,000 per photo, according to invitations sent out to potential donors. The Wall Street Journal earlier reported on the invitations.

The contribution costs are lower than normal, which appears designed to get more donors and raise higher amounts through volume. For instance, although the setting is different, getting face time with Trump at a MAGA Inc. fundraiser still costs $1 million per seat.

This is an edition of Hugo Lowell’s Inner Loop newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.
